questions.question: On a delivery run, the steady amber comes on while you still have ample distance to stop smoothly. What should you do?
options: Proceed because the light has not turned red.
Stop before the stop line.
Stop after the line if the pedestrian crossing is empty.
questions.explanation: Stop before the line when you can do so safely. The exception applies if you were already too close to stop safely when amber first appeared.

evidence.rationale: Stop before the line when you can do so safely. The exception applies if you were already too close to stop safely when amber first appeared.
evidence.scope: Steady amber at a signal-controlled junction.

questions.question: A Garda managing a junction gives you a clear signal to stop while your traffic light is green. Which instruction controls your movement?
options: The Garda’s stop signal.
The green light until it changes.
Whichever signal was given first.
questions.explanation: A Garda directing traffic takes priority over traffic lights.

evidence.rationale: A Garda directing traffic takes priority over traffic lights.
evidence.scope: A Garda is actively controlling traffic.

questions.question: Your coach is in the left-turn lane. A green left arrow is lit alongside the red main signal, and the turn is clear. What does the arrow permit?
options: Driving straight through the junction.
Waiting until the main light turns green before turning.
Turning left if it remains safe.
questions.explanation: A green filter arrow permits the indicated movement when safe, even alongside a red main signal.

evidence.rationale: A green filter arrow permits the indicated movement when safe, even alongside a red main signal.
evidence.scope: A green arrow controlling the left turn.

questions.question: The traffic lights at a junction are out of order. You are approaching the control line in a rigid truck. What does the RSA advise?
options: Treat the failed signal as a green light if you are on the wider road.
Stop at the control line, then proceed safely while yielding to traffic with right of way.
Slow down and continue without stopping if the first lane is clear.
questions.explanation: Stop at the line first. Check the whole junction and yield as required before proceeding.

evidence.rationale: Stop at the line first. Check the whole junction and yield as required before proceeding.
evidence.scope: Failed signals without a Garda directing traffic.

questions.question: Flashing red lights are showing at an automated railway crossing. The barrier has yet to close. What should you do?
options: Go through before the barrier starts moving.
Continue if you can see both ways along the tracks.
Stop safely before the crossing.
questions.explanation: Flashing red at the level crossing tells you to stop, regardless of the barrier’s position.

evidence.rationale: Flashing red at the level crossing tells you to stop, regardless of the barrier’s position.
evidence.scope: Active flashing red signals at an automated railway crossing.

questions.question: You are going straight through a yellow box. The lights are green, but the queue beyond leaves room for only the front of your vehicle. Where should you wait?
options: Inside the box with only the cab across.
Before the box until the full vehicle can clear it.
Inside the box as long as the traffic light stays green.
questions.explanation: Wait before entering. You need space to clear the box without stopping when going straight.

evidence.rationale: Wait before entering. You need space to clear the box without stopping when going straight.
evidence.scope: Straight-ahead movement, so the right-turn exception does not apply.

questions.question: You approach a stop sign with a marked line at the exit from an industrial estate. The main road appears empty. What is required at the line?
options: Slow to a crawl and continue if nobody is visible.
Stop only if another vehicle is approaching.
Come to a complete stop before continuing when safe.
questions.explanation: The stop sign requires a full stop even when the road looks empty.

evidence.rationale: The stop sign requires a full stop even when the road looks empty.
evidence.scope: A stop sign with a marked stop line.

questions.question: You are turning left at a junction and see a pedestrian already crossing the road you are entering. What should you do?
options: Wait and yield to the pedestrian.
Continue because you started indicating first.
Pass behind the pedestrian as soon as there is space for your front wheels.
questions.explanation: Give way to people already crossing at a junction before completing the turn.

evidence.rationale: Give way to people already crossing at a junction before completing the turn.
evidence.scope: The pedestrian has already started crossing.

questions.question: You are driving a coach designed for seated passengers only and towing nothing. After a lawful overtake on a two-lane motorway, where should you return once there is a safe gap?
options: Stay in the right lane until approaching an exit.
Return to the left lane when safe.
Use either lane according to which has the better road surface.
questions.explanation: Use the left lane for normal motorway driving. Return to it once the overtake is complete and it is safe.

evidence.section: Motorway safety campaign, rules of the road
evidence.rationale: Use the left lane for normal motorway driving. Return to it once the overtake is complete and it is safe.
evidence.scope: Normal motorway driving after a lawful overtake. Seated-passenger coach, no trailer.

questions.question: You signal to change lanes but a vehicle in the destination lane is still alongside your rear quarter. What should you do?
options: Move over gradually so it can slow down.
Move as soon as your indicator has flashed three times.
Hold your lane until a safe gap opens.
questions.explanation: An indicator communicates intent. Check that the lane change is safe before moving across.

evidence.rationale: An indicator communicates intent. Check that the lane change is safe before moving across.
evidence.scope: Ordinary lane change with another vehicle alongside.

questions.question: How can you measure your following gap in seconds on a dry road?
options: Count from when the vehicle ahead passes a fixed marker until you reach it.
Count from when you pass a marker until the vehicle ahead passes the next marker.
Divide the distance to the vehicle ahead by the posted limit.
questions.explanation: Use the same fixed point for both vehicles. The elapsed time is the following gap.

evidence.rationale: Use the same fixed point for both vehicles. The elapsed time is the following gap.
evidence.scope: Measuring the gap on a dry road.

questions.question: Steady rain wets the road as you follow another vehicle. How should you adjust the RSA dry-road two-second benchmark?
options: Keep it if your vehicle has ABS.
Reduce it to make the other vehicle easier to see.
Double the benchmark and increase it further if conditions demand.
questions.explanation: The RSA advises doubling the dry-road following distance in wet weather. Severe conditions can call for more space.

evidence.rationale: The RSA advises doubling the dry-road following distance in wet weather. Severe conditions can call for more space.
evidence.scope: Wet-road benchmark, adjusted for actual conditions.

questions.question: A bend hides the road ahead and you are travelling below the posted speed limit. How should you select your speed?
options: Use the posted limit because the road is dry.
Use a speed that lets you stop within the road you can see is clear.
Match the speed of the vehicle ahead without considering visibility.
questions.explanation: The visible, clear distance has to be enough to stop safely. A posted limit alone cannot tell you that.

evidence.rationale: The visible, clear distance has to be enough to stop safely. A posted limit alone cannot tell you that.
evidence.scope: Restricted forward visibility.

questions.question: Two otherwise identical journeys approach a hazard at the same speed. On one, the driver takes longer to recognise it. What changes before braking starts?
options: The vehicle covers more distance before braking.
The vehicle covers less distance before braking.
Only the distance after braking can change.
questions.explanation: While the driver is still recognising the hazard and reacting, the vehicle keeps moving.

evidence.section: Section 8, Stopping distance for cars, perception and reaction time
evidence.rationale: While the driver is still recognising the hazard and reacting, the vehicle keeps moving.
evidence.scope: Compares the distance before braking at the same speed. No car-specific distances are used.

questions.question: Two otherwise identical vehicles are travelling at the same speed and their drivers react at the same moment. Which change can reduce braking grip?
options: The driver choosing an earlier time to start the shift.
The vehicle behind leaving a larger gap.
A slippery surface under the tyres.
questions.explanation: Available tyre grip affects braking capability. A slippery surface reduces the grip available.

evidence.section: Section 8, Stopping distance for cars and skidding
evidence.rationale: Available tyre grip affects braking capability. A slippery surface reduces the grip available.
evidence.scope: General grip principle without vehicle-specific stopping figures.

questions.question: You see a queue building well ahead on a straight road. Which approach best demonstrates forward planning?
options: Hold speed until close to the queue, then brake firmly.
Ease off early and slow progressively.
Accelerate into the free space before braking.
questions.explanation: Spotting the queue early gives you time to ease off and avoid late, harsh braking.

evidence.rationale: Spotting the queue early gives you time to ease off and avoid late, harsh braking.
evidence.scope: A developing queue far enough ahead for gradual deceleration.

questions.question: On the last leg of a journey you find yourself fighting sleep. What is the first priority?
options: Open a window and complete the leg without stopping.
Arrange a break after the last stop.
Pull into a safe place and stop driving.
questions.explanation: The RSA’s first step for tired drivers is to park safely. Plan a break before continuing.

evidence.rationale: The RSA’s first step for tired drivers is to park safely. Plan a break before continuing.
evidence.scope: Immediate response to fighting sleep.

questions.question: After leaving a patch of dense fog, you are driving in clear weather again. What should you do with the fog lights?
options: Turn them off.
Leave them on until the next stop.
Leave them on if another vehicle is behind you.
questions.explanation: Switch off fog lights in clear weather. They can dazzle other drivers.

evidence.rationale: Switch off fog lights in clear weather. They can dazzle other drivers.
evidence.scope: Conditions have cleared and there is no falling snow.

questions.question: The lights change and you can move off safely in a coach. Which technique follows the RSA eco-driving guidance?
options: Build high revs while stationary to move off faster.
Pull away smoothly with progressive accelerator input.
Accelerate hard initially and then coast to settle speed.
questions.explanation: Smooth, progressive acceleration avoids unnecessary engine revs and abrupt changes in speed.

evidence.rationale: Smooth, progressive acceleration avoids unnecessary engine revs and abrupt changes in speed.
evidence.scope: Normal departure in a coach when safe to move off.

questions.question: Heavy rain starts while your truck’s cruise control is active. What does the RSA recommend?
options: Disengage cruise control and manage speed directly.
Keep cruise control on but lower the setting.
Use cruise control until standing water is visible.
questions.explanation: The RSA advises avoiding cruise control in heavy rain because it can reduce control and affect your reaction to hazards.

evidence.rationale: The RSA advises avoiding cruise control in heavy rain because it can reduce control and affect your reaction to hazards.
evidence.scope: Heavy rain, even without visible standing water.

questions.question: Following a motorway breakdown, you and your occupants can exit safely and there is a crash barrier next to the hard shoulder. Where should you wait for help?
options: Just in front of the vehicle on the shoulder.
Between the vehicle and the carriageway.
Well behind the barrier on the embankment side.
questions.explanation: Wait away from the live traffic area, behind the crash barrier where available.

evidence.rationale: Wait away from the live traffic area, behind the crash barrier where available.
evidence.scope: Everyone can safely leave and get behind the barrier.

questions.question: You have broken down on a motorway and cannot safely follow the RSA advice to leave the vehicle. How should you wait while getting help?
options: Remain belted in the vehicle with hazard lights on.
Wait unbelted so you can move more quickly.
Stand beside the vehicle nearest to live traffic.
questions.explanation: When it is unsafe to follow the exit advice, the RSA advises staying belted inside with the hazards on.

evidence.rationale: When it is unsafe to follow the exit advice, the RSA advises staying belted inside with the hazards on.
evidence.scope: Safe exit advice cannot be followed.

questions.question: From a safe place you report a motorway breakdown. Which information from a roadside location marker is especially useful?
options: The speed limit for the road.
The location reference and direction of travel.
The permitted gross weight of your vehicle.
questions.explanation: The location reference and direction help responders find the correct stretch of road.

evidence.section: Section 11, Location reference indicators and markings
evidence.rationale: The location reference and direction help responders find the correct stretch of road.
evidence.scope: A location marker is visible from a safe place.

questions.question: Your vehicle has stopped following a breakdown in a tunnel. You can safely reach an emergency station. Which phone should you use to alert the tunnel operator?
options: The tunnel emergency station phone.
A passenger’s phone to call the next toll plaza.
A phone at the first service area outside the tunnel.
questions.explanation: The emergency station phone puts you in contact with the tunnel operator.

evidence.section: Section 11, Tunnels, Breakdown or a crash
evidence.rationale: The emergency station phone puts you in contact with the tunnel operator.
evidence.scope: You can safely reach a tunnel emergency station.

questions.question: You miss your motorway exit while trying to reach a service area. What is the safe way to correct the route?
options: Reverse along the hard shoulder to the exit.
Turn at the next gap in the central barrier.
Continue to a suitable exit ahead.
questions.explanation: Motorway rules prohibit turning or reversing. Continue ahead until you can leave by an exit.

evidence.section: Motorway safety campaign, rules of the road
evidence.rationale: Motorway rules prohibit turning or reversing. Continue ahead until you can leave by an exit.
evidence.scope: Ordinary missed exit, without an emergency or Garda instruction.

questions.question: A four-axle goods vehicle reaches a timed prohibition for goods vehicles with three or more axles. The restriction is in force and the driver has no permit. What should the driver do?
options: Proceed because the sign only applies to vehicles with exactly three axles.
Proceed if the vehicle is running empty.
Take a route that avoids the restriction.
questions.explanation: The axle symbol sets a threshold. Vehicles at or above it need a permit while the restriction is active.

evidence.rationale: The axle symbol sets a threshold. Vehicles at or above it need a permit while the restriction is active.
evidence.scope: Applies to a goods vehicle during the times shown.

questions.question: On a 2-plus-1 road, the only way to pass a slow vehicle would involve driving across the hatched central median. What should you do?
options: Stay in your lane until there is a lawful opportunity to pass.
Use the median if you can see a clear gap on the other side.
Enter the median while indicating and move back as soon as possible.
questions.explanation: The hatched median separates opposing traffic and must be kept clear.

evidence.rationale: The hatched median separates opposing traffic and must be kept clear.
evidence.scope: A central median separating opposite directions.

questions.question: A road worker displays the Stop side of a paddle at a single-lane works site. A vehicle in front of you has just been allowed through. What should you do?
options: Follow the other vehicle before oncoming traffic arrives.
Continue at walking speed if the lane appears empty.
Stop and wait for Go.
questions.explanation: The paddle controls when your vehicle may pass. The previous vehicle’s permission does not carry over.

evidence.section: Section 6, Stop and Go traffic control at roadworks
evidence.rationale: The paddle controls when your vehicle may pass. The previous vehicle’s permission does not carry over.
evidence.scope: Manually controlled stop-and-go roadworks.

questions.question: On approach to a motorway exit, you pass the blue countdown sign with one white diagonal bar. How far away is the exit indicated by the sign?
options: 200 metres.
300 metres.
100 metres.
questions.explanation: One bar indicates 100 metres. The corresponding signs with two and three bars show 200 and 300 metres.

evidence.rationale: One bar indicates 100 metres. The corresponding signs with two and three bars show 200 and 300 metres.
evidence.scope: Standard motorway exit countdown sign.

questions.question: A tunnel’s variable speed sign shows 50 km/h in a red circle. What does the number mean while it is displayed?
options: It is the displayed road limit. A lower applicable vehicle limit still applies.
It is the recommended minimum to keep traffic moving.
It is advisory unless a separate fixed sign also shows 50.
questions.explanation: An active regulatory display sets the road speed limit. A lower vehicle-specific limit takes precedence, and conditions can require a lower speed.

evidence.section: Section 11, Driving in a tunnel; Section 8, Speed limits for vehicles
evidence.rationale: An active regulatory display sets the road speed limit. A lower vehicle-specific limit takes precedence, and conditions can require a lower speed.
evidence.scope: A regulatory electronic display showing a number in a red circle.

questions.question: The kerb has a single yellow line and a plate prohibiting parking from 08:00 to 10:00. You want to park there at 09:30. What does this marking tell you?
options: Parking is permitted as long as a space is free.
The restriction begins at 10:00.
Parking is prohibited at that time.
questions.explanation: The plate gives the times during which the yellow-line parking restriction applies.

evidence.rationale: The plate gives the times during which the yellow-line parking restriction applies.
evidence.scope: Concerns ordinary parking during the hours shown.

questions.question: A metered bay lies within a clearway during its signed operating hours. Can you park there if the meter still takes payment?
options: No. The clearway restriction applies even when metered parking is normally available.
Yes, if payment is made before leaving the vehicle.
Yes, if you remain with the vehicle.
questions.explanation: The clearway keeps the road available to traffic during the hours on its sign.

evidence.rationale: The clearway keeps the road available to traffic during the hours on its sign.
evidence.scope: Ordinary parking during an active clearway.

questions.question: The vehicle signal at a pelican crossing is flashing amber while someone is still crossing. What should you do?
options: Wait and let the person clear your path.
Proceed slowly if the pedestrian is halfway across.
Sound your horn and then drive on.
questions.explanation: Flashing amber requires drivers to give way to pedestrians who are crossing.

evidence.section: Section 7, Traffic lights; Section 18, Pelican crossing
evidence.rationale: Flashing amber requires drivers to give way to pedestrians who are crossing.
evidence.scope: Pelican crossing with a pedestrian on the crossing.

questions.question: At the entrance to a street you see a red circular sign with a horizontal white bar. What does it mean for your vehicle?
options: No entry from this end.
Two-way traffic begins here.
Only goods vehicles are prohibited.
questions.explanation: The white bar on a red circular background marks a no-entry point for vehicles.

evidence.rationale: The white bar on a red circular background marks a no-entry point for vehicles.
evidence.scope: Standard no-entry sign without a permitted exception.

questions.question: Your vehicle is too long to fit completely within the median at a dual carriageway junction. How should you plan to turn right from the minor road?
options: Use the median even if the rear remains in a live lane.
Enter the near carriageway and use your indicators to hold traffic while you wait.
Wait on the minor road for a gap that lets you complete the whole turn.
questions.explanation: The vehicle needs a gap across both carriageways when it cannot wait clear of live lanes in the median.

evidence.section: Section 9, Crossing a dual carriageway or joining it by turning right
evidence.rationale: The vehicle needs a gap across both carriageways when it cannot wait clear of live lanes in the median.
evidence.scope: Minor-road right turn with a median shorter than the vehicle.

questions.question: The approach arrows direct traffic for your exit into a different lane from the one suggested by the general clock-face rule. Which should guide your approach?
options: The clock-face rule regardless of local markings.
The lane chosen by the vehicle in front.
The arrows and markings for that roundabout.
questions.explanation: The general rule is a planning aid. Follow the directions marked for the junction you are using.

evidence.rationale: The general rule is a planning aid. Follow the directions marked for the junction you are using.
evidence.scope: Roundabout with clear lane instructions.

questions.question: You are at the entry to an unsignalised roundabout. A vehicle on the roundabout is approaching your entry from the right. Who should wait?
options: The other driver should yield because you are at the entry line first.
You should yield to the vehicle already on the roundabout.
Whichever driver is taking the later exit should wait.
questions.explanation: Yield to traffic coming from the right or already circulating as you approach.

evidence.rationale: Yield to traffic coming from the right or already circulating as you approach.
evidence.scope: Unsignalised entry without a Garda or contrary direction.

questions.question: You are taking the second exit straight ahead at a roundabout with standard lane markings. When should you normally begin signalling left?
options: After passing the exit immediately before yours.
Before entering the roundabout.
As soon as you pass the stop or yield line on entry.
questions.explanation: Signal left after passing the preceding exit so others can identify the exit you intend to take.

evidence.section: Section 9, Going straight ahead at roundabouts
evidence.rationale: Signal left after passing the preceding exit so others can identify the exit you intend to take.
evidence.scope: Straight-ahead second exit, with no contrary lane or signal instructions.

questions.question: You discover that a minor road is too narrow to turn around at its junction with a major road. Is reversing out onto the major road the right approach?
options: No. Find a safe way to leave the minor road driving forwards.
Yes, if you use hazard lights.
Yes, if there is a gap in traffic from one direction.
questions.explanation: The RSA prohibits reversing from a minor road onto a major road because of the danger to other traffic.

evidence.rationale: The RSA prohibits reversing from a minor road onto a major road because of the danger to other traffic.
evidence.scope: Ordinary road junction.

questions.question: Your slip road is ending and a car is already alongside you in the motorway’s left lane. Who should yield during the merge?
options: The car must slow because you are on an acceleration lane.
The driver with the smaller vehicle should yield.
You should yield to traffic already on the motorway.
questions.explanation: Use the slip road to look for a suitable gap and yield to vehicles already on the motorway.

evidence.rationale: Use the slip road to look for a suitable gap and yield to vehicles already on the motorway.
evidence.scope: An acceleration lane that merges into an existing motorway lane.

questions.question: There is no upright parking restriction sign, but your proposed stopping place is within the zig-zag markings at a zebra crossing. May you park there?
options: Yes, provided the crossing stripes themselves are clear.
Yes, if the delivery takes less than a minute.
No. The crossing’s zig-zag markings prohibit parking there.
questions.explanation: The parking prohibition includes the marked approach and departure area at the crossing.

evidence.rationale: The parking prohibition includes the marked approach and departure area at the crossing.
evidence.scope: Ordinary parking within crossing zig-zags.

questions.question: You have missed a turn on a one-way street. What should you do to correct your route?
options: Continue in the permitted direction and find a legal route back.
Make a U-turn when no vehicle is approaching.
Turn around as long as hazard lights are on.
questions.explanation: A U-turn would put the vehicle against the permitted direction. Continue and reroute.

evidence.rationale: A U-turn would put the vehicle against the permitted direction. Continue and reroute.
evidence.scope: Ordinary one-way street with no authorised direction to turn.

questions.question: A goods vehicle with a maximum authorised mass of 12 tonnes is following slower traffic on a three-lane motorway. No obstruction prevents progress in the inner lanes. Can it use the outside lane to overtake?
options: Yes, as long as it is carrying less than 3.5 tonnes of cargo.
No. The outside lane restriction applies to that goods vehicle.
Yes, if it moves back to the middle lane promptly.
questions.explanation: The restriction uses maximum authorised mass, not the load carried. An obstruction exception does not apply merely because traffic is slower.

evidence.rationale: The restriction uses maximum authorised mass, not the load carried. An obstruction exception does not apply merely because traffic is slower.
evidence.scope: Goods vehicle over 3,500 kg, ordinary overtaking, no obstruction.

questions.question: You discover a defect during your vehicle inspection. Alongside its description and the time and date, what should the record include if applicable?
options: Any temporary measure taken to reduce the defect’s effect.
The planned delivery order for the day.
Only the date of the previous service.
questions.explanation: The defect report documents temporary mitigation along with the finding and when it was made.

evidence.section: Obligations in relation to recording of defects
evidence.rationale: The defect report documents temporary mitigation along with the finding and when it was made.
evidence.scope: Commercial vehicle inspection where a defect was found.

questions.question: A colleague has never been trained to check your class of commercial vehicle. Should the operator assign them the pre-use inspection without training?
options: No. The person who carries out the checks needs appropriate training.
Yes, provided they hold a full car licence.
Yes, provided the vehicle has a current roadworthiness certificate.
questions.explanation: The check may be carried out by a trained person, such as a trained driver or mechanic.

evidence.section: What do daily walk around checks entail?
evidence.rationale: The check may be carried out by a trained person, such as a trained driver or mechanic.
evidence.scope: Applies to commercial vehicle walk-around inspections.

questions.question: A commercial vehicle defect has been repaired after a report. Where should the corrective action be recorded?
options: In the vehicle’s maintenance record.
Only in the driver’s delivery notes.
Only on the next annual test application.
questions.explanation: Recording the corrective action in the maintenance record links the defect to its follow-up.

evidence.rationale: Recording the corrective action in the maintenance record links the defect to its follow-up.
evidence.scope: Operator record-keeping after corrective work.

questions.question: A fleet manager wants to rely on planned maintenance alone and end pre-use walk-arounds. Which statement reflects CVRT guidance?
options: Daily walk-arounds are required only during the month before a test.
The maintenance system needs both planned inspections and daily walk-arounds.
Planned maintenance can replace the walk-around if no faults were reported on the previous shift.
questions.explanation: Pre-use checks and planned preventative maintenance are separate parts of the inspection system.

evidence.rationale: Pre-use checks and planned preventative maintenance are separate parts of the inspection system.
evidence.scope: Commercial vehicle maintenance system.

questions.question: During a journey you find a fault likely to put other road users in danger. What should you do first?
options: Carry on slowly to the next scheduled customer.
Finish the route and record the fault on return.
Stop driving as soon as you can do so at a safe location.
questions.explanation: A dangerous fault requires stopping at a safe place and obtaining suitable inspection before driving again.

evidence.section: Detection of defects by drivers when on the road
evidence.rationale: A dangerous fault requires stopping at a safe place and obtaining suitable inspection before driving again.
evidence.scope: A fault likely to create danger while the vehicle is in motion.

questions.question: Salt spray has made a side mirror difficult to use before your shift. What should you do before driving?
options: Clean it and make sure it is correctly positioned.
Leave it because the other mirror gives a view to the rear.
Move it further out so more of the mirror faces the light.
questions.explanation: A mirror needs a clear surface and correct position to give effective observations.

evidence.rationale: A mirror needs a clear surface and correct position to give effective observations.
evidence.scope: A fitted side mirror obscured by dirt.

questions.question: You find a loose water bottle on the floor near the coach pedals. What should you do before moving?
options: Roll it behind the accelerator to keep it out of the aisle.
Leave it on the floor as long as it is behind your heel.
Stow it securely away from the foot controls.
questions.explanation: Loose equipment can move under a pedal and interfere with control.

evidence.rationale: Loose equipment can move under a pedal and interfere with control.
evidence.scope: Loose item in the driver’s footwell.

questions.question: A pallet load is ready to go in a curtain-sided trailer with ordinary weather curtains. Can the closed curtains serve as the load restraint?
options: No. Use a restraint system suitable for the load.
Yes, if the buckles are all tight.
Yes, if the load will remain on the trailer for only one stop.
questions.explanation: Standard curtains protect the load from weather and are not a substitute for rated restraint.

evidence.rationale: Standard curtains protect the load from weather and are not a substitute for rated restraint.
evidence.scope: Ordinary weather curtains, with no certified load-bearing system.

questions.question: An operator fits XL-labelled curtains to a trailer with an unrated body. Can the retrofit alone establish an XL-rated restraint system?
options: Yes, if the curtain label is visible on both sides.
Yes, if the operator uses the same buckles supplied with the curtains.
No. The rating concerns the complete structure and curtains together.
questions.explanation: The structural rating applies to a system. Fitting a rated component does not establish the rating of the whole vehicle body.

evidence.rationale: The structural rating applies to a system. Fitting a rated component does not establish the rating of the whole vehicle body.
evidence.scope: Existing trailer body without an XL rating.

questions.question: A heavy pallet is resting on the load bed without restraint. A colleague says its weight will keep it in place. What is the concern?
options: Movement over the road can reduce contact and friction, allowing the pallet to shift.
A heavier pallet always increases grip enough to prevent movement.
A pallet only shifts if another object hits it.
questions.explanation: The weight alone cannot be relied on. Contact and friction can be lost when a pallet lifts or bounces.

evidence.rationale: The weight alone cannot be relied on. Contact and friction can be lost when a pallet lifts or bounces.
evidence.scope: Palletised load on a trailer bed.

questions.question: What does suitable anti-slip matting between a pallet and the load bed contribute to the securing plan?
options: It increases friction and can affect the number of lashings needed.
It increases the permitted axle load.
It makes every load self-securing once the vehicle reaches road speed.
questions.explanation: Anti-slip matting improves friction. The rest of the restraint plan still depends on the load and securing calculation.

evidence.rationale: Anti-slip matting improves friction. The rest of the restraint plan still depends on the load and securing calculation.
evidence.scope: A calculated restraint plan for a palletised load.

questions.question: A suitable headboard is part of a securing plan and the load is positioned against it. Which movement is that headboard designed to help prevent?
options: The load sliding forwards under braking.
The load rolling backwards as the truck accelerates.
The load moving upwards when it crosses a bump.
questions.explanation: A suitable front headboard provides forward blocking. Other directions need their own restraint.

evidence.rationale: A suitable front headboard provides forward blocking. Other directions need their own restraint.
evidence.scope: Appropriately rated headboard used within its capacity.

questions.question: A load plan relies on positive fit, but there is a large open gap between the pallet group and the blocking structure. What should you do?
options: Leave the gap so the pallets can settle during the first part of the trip.
Rely on the curtains to absorb any movement across the gap.
Have the restraint plan corrected before departure.
questions.explanation: Blocking relies on a close fit. A large gap allows the load to build up movement before it reaches the structure.

evidence.rationale: Blocking relies on a close fit. A large gap allows the load to build up movement before it reaches the structure.
evidence.scope: Positive-fit restraint for a curtain-sided pallet load.

questions.question: Before reversing a tractor unit towards a stationary semi-trailer for a conventional fifth-wheel coupling, which trailer control should you check?
options: The trailer parking brake is released.
The tractor parking brake is the only brake that matters.
The trailer parking brake is applied.
questions.explanation: An applied trailer parking brake helps prevent the semi-trailer moving during coupling.

evidence.rationale: An applied trailer parking brake helps prevent the semi-trailer moving during coupling.
evidence.scope: Conventional fifth-wheel procedure. Follow vehicle and operator instructions.

questions.question: What should you check about a semi-trailer’s height before reversing a tractor unit into the coupling position?
options: The trailer bed is level with the tractor roof.
The trailer height is suitable for the tractor unit to receive it safely.
The trailer is as high as its landing gear will allow.
questions.explanation: The procedure calls for checking that the fifth wheel can receive the trailer correctly at its set height.

evidence.rationale: The procedure calls for checking that the fifth wheel can receive the trailer correctly at its set height.
evidence.scope: Conventional fifth-wheel combination.

questions.question: A fifth-wheel coupling has a safety clip for the kingpin release handle. What is the clip’s purpose in the coupling checks?
options: Hold the landing gear at road height.
Secure the release handle after coupling.
Lock the electrical connector to its socket.
questions.explanation: The safety clip secures the kingpin release handle in the locking assembly.

evidence.rationale: The safety clip secures the kingpin release handle in the locking assembly.
evidence.scope: Equipment fitted with the specified clip.

questions.question: Which equipment supports the front of a conventional semi-trailer once the tractor unit is moved clear?
options: The air and electrical lines until they are disconnected.
The trailer landing gear, lowered to support the trailer.
The tractor’s fifth wheel after the tractor has moved away.
questions.explanation: The landing gear provides support before the tractor moves clear.

evidence.rationale: The landing gear provides support before the tractor moves clear.
evidence.scope: Conventional semi-trailer, operator’s uncoupling sequence applies.

questions.question: You have connected the trailer electrical line. What should you do before taking the combination onto the road?
options: Check that the trailer lights operate.
Assume a locked electrical plug confirms every lamp is working.
Wait for the first stop to check the lights after they have warmed up.
questions.explanation: Connecting the electrical line enables the lights. A function check is still needed.

evidence.rationale: Connecting the electrical line enables the lights. A function check is still needed.
evidence.scope: A newly coupled tractor and semi-trailer.

questions.question: An in-scope driver drove 54 hours last week. Subject to all other limits, what is the most they can drive this week?
options: 42 hours.
56 hours.
36 hours.
questions.explanation: The consecutive-week total cannot exceed 90 hours. After 54 hours that leaves 36.

evidence.rationale: The consecutive-week total cannot exceed 90 hours. After 54 hours that leaves 36.
evidence.scope: Standard EU rule. Consider only the two-week driving total in this calculation.

questions.question: A dispatcher schedules 58 driving hours in one week and 30 the next. The driver is subject to standard EU rules. What is wrong with the schedule?
options: It is compliant because the two-week total is 88 hours.
Only the 30-hour week is a problem because each week must have at least 45 hours of driving.
The 58-hour week exceeds the weekly limit even though the combined total is below 90.
questions.explanation: The weekly ceiling is 56 hours and applies independently of the two-week ceiling.

evidence.rationale: The weekly ceiling is 56 hours and applies independently of the two-week ceiling.
evidence.scope: Standard EU rule. The figures are driving hours only.

questions.question: A truck driver used ten-hour driving days on Monday and Wednesday. What is the standard maximum driving time on Friday of the same week?
options: Nine and a half hours.
Nine hours.
Ten hours if the driver takes a longer break.
questions.explanation: A driver may extend daily driving to ten hours at most twice in a week. Both extensions have already been used.

evidence.rationale: A driver may extend daily driving to ten hours at most twice in a week. Both extensions have already been used.
evidence.scope: In scope and no derogation.

questions.question: You spend 45 minutes unloading between driving periods. Why can that time not count as the driving break?
options: It can count if the vehicle’s engine is switched off.
Unloading is work, and a driving break is time for recuperation free from work.
It can count if a different company owns the goods.
questions.explanation: A driving break excludes both driving and other work.

evidence.rationale: A driving break excludes both driving and other work.
evidence.scope: Standard EU rule. The driver personally unloads.

questions.question: On an in-scope goods run you want to split the standard driving break. Which sequence meets the minimum lengths in the required order?
options: At least 30 minutes, then at least 15 minutes.
At least 15 minutes, then at least 30 minutes.
At least 20 minutes, then at least 25 minutes.
questions.explanation: The standard two-part option requires the longer minimum for the second break.

evidence.rationale: The standard two-part option requires the longer minimum for the second break.
evidence.scope: Standard goods rule, with the breaks taken at the appropriate points in the driving period.

questions.question: On an in-scope occasional coach service you plan two breaks of 20 and 25 minutes. Assuming they are correctly timed, can this meet the occasional-service split option?
options: No. The second break must be 30 minutes for every passenger service.
Yes. Each break is at least 15 minutes and the total is 45 minutes.
No. Each break must be at least 30 minutes on an occasional service.
questions.explanation: The occasional-passenger option allows two breaks of at least 15 minutes each that together meet the 45-minute requirement.

evidence.rationale: The occasional-passenger option allows two breaks of at least 15 minutes each that together meet the 45-minute requirement.
evidence.scope: A qualifying occasional passenger service. All timing and documentation requirements still apply.

questions.question: A bus operates a regular passenger service over a 40 km route. What does Regulation 561/2006 say about its scope?
options: It applies to all bus services with more than eight passenger seats, regardless of route.
The regulation exempts that service. Applicable national driving and rest rules still apply.
It exempts the route only if the bus carries no standing passengers.
questions.explanation: Article 3(a) exempts regular passenger services on routes no longer than 50 km. Article 15 requires national driving-time, break and rest protections for these drivers.

evidence.rationale: Article 3(a) exempts regular passenger services on routes no longer than 50 km. Article 15 requires national driving-time, break and rest protections for these drivers.
evidence.scope: Route length refers to the regular service, not just a driver’s individual portion.

questions.question: An in-scope driver has already taken three reduced daily rest periods since the last weekly rest. Under standard rules, can they schedule another before the next weekly rest?
options: Yes, as long as the previous two reduced rests were not consecutive.
No. The allowance is three between weekly rest periods.
Yes, if the next driving day stays below nine hours.
questions.explanation: Three reduced daily rests is the maximum between any two weekly rest periods.

evidence.rationale: Three reduced daily rests is the maximum between any two weekly rest periods.
evidence.scope: Standard rule without a relevant derogation.

questions.question: A weekly rest starts on Sunday evening and continues into Monday. How may it be assigned when checking weekly rest compliance?
options: To either of the weeks, once.
Only to the week in which it ends.
To both weeks if enough hours fall in each.
questions.explanation: A weekly rest spanning two weeks can be counted for one week or the other.

evidence.rationale: A weekly rest spanning two weeks can be counted for one week or the other.
evidence.scope: A single qualifying weekly rest that spans the week boundary.

questions.question: An in-scope driver plans to take a regular 45-hour weekly rest while parked in a sleeper cab at a depot. Is that allowed under the standard rule?
options: No. Regular weekly rest must be taken in suitable accommodation outside the vehicle.
Yes, because the vehicle is parked at a depot.
Yes, if the driver has a proper bunk in the cab.
questions.explanation: The regular weekly rest cannot be taken in a vehicle, even if it is stationary and has a bunk.

evidence.rationale: The regular weekly rest cannot be taken in a vehicle, even if it is stationary and has a bunk.
evidence.scope: Ordinary weekly rest without a ferry or train situation.

questions.question: Which pair of uninterrupted periods can make a split regular daily rest if completed within the applicable time window?
options: Six hours followed by six hours.
Three hours followed by nine hours.
Nine hours followed by three hours.
questions.explanation: A split regular daily rest requires a first period of at least three hours and a second of at least nine.

evidence.rationale: A split regular daily rest requires a first period of at least three hours and a second of at least nine.
evidence.scope: Standard split regular daily rest. Timing under Article 8 still applies.

questions.question: What minimum following distance does the RSA recommend for a truck or bus moving through a tunnel, before any larger gap the conditions or signs call for?
options: 50 metres.
25 metres.
100 metres.
questions.explanation: The tunnel guidance gives 100 metres for vehicles other than cars and motorcycles.

evidence.rationale: The tunnel guidance gives 100 metres for vehicles other than cars and motorcycles.
evidence.scope: An Irish road tunnel, with signs and conditions still governing the actual gap.

questions.question: Two drivers press the brake at the same point. One braking system takes longer to respond. What can that delay change?
options: It can only affect the driver’s ability to see a hazard.
It can increase the distance covered before effective braking begins.
It has no bearing on the distance needed to stop.
questions.explanation: Vehicle response contributes to stopping distance as well as the driver’s reaction and available braking grip.

evidence.section: Section 8, Stopping distance for cars, Vehicle reaction and braking capability
evidence.rationale: Vehicle response contributes to stopping distance as well as the driver’s reaction and available braking grip.
evidence.scope: General principle. No vehicle-specific stopping-distance figure is implied.

questions.question: You are following a vehicle on a road with icy patches. How should you treat the ordinary dry-road following gap?
options: Use the dry-road minimum as long as you have ABS.
Allow considerably more space to account for reduced grip.
Follow closer to stay within the other vehicle’s tyre tracks.
questions.explanation: Icy conditions may require much more following distance than the dry-road benchmark.

evidence.rationale: Icy conditions may require much more following distance than the dry-road benchmark.
evidence.scope: Icy conditions where it is otherwise safe to travel.

questions.question: What happens when a vehicle aquaplanes on standing water?
options: Water increases grip because it cools the tyres.
Only the visibility through the windscreen changes.
Water separates the tyres from the road, reducing steering and braking control.
questions.explanation: A layer of water can lift the tyres away from the road surface and reduce control.

evidence.rationale: A layer of water can lift the tyres away from the road surface and reduce control.
evidence.scope: General effect of aquaplaning.

questions.question: Light is fading and your vehicle is using daytime running lights alone. What should you switch to at lighting-up time?
options: Daytime running lights and hazard lights together.
Main beam throughout the journey.
Dipped headlights.
questions.explanation: Daytime running lights are intended for daylight. Dipped headlights let you see and be seen when the light fades.

evidence.rationale: Daytime running lights are intended for daylight. Dipped headlights let you see and be seen when the light fades.
evidence.scope: Ordinary dusk driving.

questions.question: At night, you are using main beam on an unlit road and see an oncoming vehicle. Which lighting change is appropriate?
options: Dip your headlights in time to avoid dazzling the oncoming driver.
Switch to sidelights only until it has passed.
Keep main beam on because the road has no street lights.
questions.explanation: Dipped headlights are appropriate when meeting other traffic, even on an unlit road.

evidence.rationale: Dipped headlights are appropriate when meeting other traffic, even on an unlit road.
evidence.scope: Ordinary oncoming traffic at night.

questions.question: Oncoming headlights dazzle you on a dark rural road. What should you do if your view ahead is seriously reduced?
options: Maintain your speed to avoid surprising traffic behind.
Look directly into the headlights until your eyes adjust.
Slow down and stop if necessary, watching for anyone near the verge.
questions.explanation: Reduce speed when glare limits your view. Be especially alert for people near the road edge.

evidence.section: Section 5, What to do if you are dazzled
evidence.rationale: Reduce speed when glare limits your view. Be especially alert for people near the road edge.
evidence.scope: Glare from oncoming traffic. Stop safely if needed.

questions.question: A driver thinks they cannot have a microsleep as long as their eyes stay open. What does the RSA explain?
options: A microsleep requires the eyes to be closed for at least a minute.
A microsleep affects passengers but not a person actively steering.
A microsleep can happen with the eyes open.
questions.explanation: An open-eyed driver can still briefly lose awareness and control when very tired.

evidence.rationale: An open-eyed driver can still briefly lose awareness and control when very tired.
evidence.scope: Driver fatigue and short involuntary sleep.

questions.question: A coach is parked at its stand between services. Under normal conditions, what does the RSA guidance advise about idling there?
options: Switch the engine off while parked.
Keep it idling because the route is scheduled to restart.
Rev it periodically to keep fuel consumption steady.
questions.explanation: Switching off at a stand reduces avoidable fuel use, noise and local pollution.

evidence.section: Running of engines at bus stands or bus terminus
evidence.rationale: Switching off at a stand reduces avoidable fuel use, noise and local pollution.
evidence.scope: Normal stationary wait with no operational need to run the engine.

questions.question: A dispatcher says any dangerous goods carried in packages automatically require the same ADR certificate as a tank operation. What should the driver check?
options: Only whether the packages fit on a single pallet.
The rules for the goods, packaging, quantities and relevant exemptions.
Only whether the journey stays within one county.
questions.explanation: HSA distinguishes tank and packaged operations and describes exemptions for certain packaged loads.

evidence.rationale: HSA distinguishes tank and packaged operations and describes exemptions for certain packaged loads.
evidence.scope: General awareness only. A particular load requires current specialist advice.

questions.question: Who can an operator consult for specialist advice on its responsibilities when carrying dangerous goods by road?
options: A general vehicle test booking clerk.
The person responsible only for road toll accounts.
A qualified Dangerous Goods Safety Adviser.
questions.explanation: A Dangerous Goods Safety Adviser can help an undertaking manage its dangerous-goods responsibilities.

evidence.rationale: A Dangerous Goods Safety Adviser can help an undertaking manage its dangerous-goods responsibilities.
evidence.scope: General specialist referral, within the adviser’s certified classes.

questions.question: Your bus has stopped at an authorised stop. What should you do with the brake before opening the passenger doors?
options: Apply the handbrake or bus-stop brake as appropriate.
Release the brake so the vehicle can settle against the kerb.
Wait until passengers have begun boarding before applying it.
questions.explanation: Secure the stationary bus before opening its doors to passengers.

evidence.rationale: Secure the stationary bus before opening its doors to passengers.
evidence.scope: Normal service stop, subject to vehicle and operator procedures.

questions.question: Before opening the doors of a stationary bus, why should you check the area on the door side?
options: To make sure door operation and access will not put anyone in danger.
To check whether the next bus has left the depot.
To judge the distance from following vehicles in the overtaking lane.
questions.explanation: The nearside check helps identify anyone or anything in the area affected by the doors.

evidence.rationale: The nearside check helps identify anyone or anything in the area affected by the doors.
evidence.scope: Bus already stationary and secured.

questions.question: A passenger who needs extra time is still making their way to a seat after boarding. What should the driver do?
options: Move off as soon as the doors close.
Allow them time to get settled before moving off.
Ask them to sit while the bus accelerates.
questions.explanation: Allowing passengers time to settle reduces the chance of a fall when the bus starts moving.

evidence.rationale: Allowing passengers time to settle reduces the chance of a fall when the bus starts moving.
evidence.scope: A normal service stop where waiting for the passenger is possible.

questions.question: A wheelchair user has boarded and the ramp is stowed. What still needs checking before departure?
options: They are safely accommodated according to the vehicle’s wheelchair-space procedure.
The wheelchair user can reach the ticket machine from the space.
The ramp’s use alone confirms the passenger is ready.
questions.explanation: Stowing a ramp does not complete the passenger safety check. Confirm the wheelchair space is used correctly for the bus.

evidence.rationale: Stowing a ramp does not complete the passenger safety check. Confirm the wheelchair space is used correctly for the bus.
evidence.scope: Accessible bus with vehicle-specific wheelchair procedures.

questions.question: Bags have been placed in front of a coach emergency exit. What should happen before the coach departs?
options: Move and stow the bags so the exit remains accessible.
Leave them if passengers are told to use the main door.
Leave them if the driver can reach the bags from the front.
questions.explanation: Emergency exits must remain accessible because the main door may be unusable in an emergency.

evidence.rationale: Emergency exits must remain accessible because the main door may be unusable in an emergency.
evidence.scope: Passenger vehicle with an emergency exit.

questions.question: You are assigned a bus with a wheelchair lift you have not used before. What should be part of your preparation before service?
options: Learn the operator’s procedure and confirm that the lift operates properly.
Wait for the first passenger to show you how to use it.
Assume all wheelchair lifts have the same controls.
questions.explanation: The RSA includes accessible equipment in pre-use checks. Use the procedure for the specific vehicle.

evidence.rationale: The RSA includes accessible equipment in pre-use checks. Use the procedure for the specific vehicle.
evidence.scope: Bus fitted with a wheelchair lift.

questions.question: When taking charge of an unfamiliar bus, why should you identify its emergency engine and fuel cut-offs?
options: To use them as the normal controls when approaching a bus stop.
To adjust the running fuel consumption between stops.
To know how to stop the engine or fuel supply if an emergency requires it.
questions.explanation: Emergency cut-offs let the driver isolate the engine or fuel supply when appropriate.

evidence.section: Engine and fuel cut off, page 36
evidence.rationale: Emergency cut-offs let the driver isolate the engine or fuel supply when appropriate.
evidence.scope: Vehicle fitted with emergency engine and fuel controls.

questions.question: A colleague proposes using a weight figure from a different truck to decide whether your loaded combination is legal. What should you do?
options: Use the other figure if both vehicles are operated by the same company.
Check the limits for your particular vehicle combination and design.
Use the other figure if both trailers have the same number of axles.
questions.explanation: Legal limits can vary with the configuration and design. Check the actual combination.

evidence.section: Frequently asked questions, How do I know if the load exceeds legal limits?
evidence.rationale: Legal limits can vary with the configuration and design. Check the actual combination.
evidence.scope: Commercial goods vehicles with potentially different configurations.

questions.question: A vehicle is within its overall gross limit but one axle exceeds the applicable limit. Is the load acceptable as it stands?
options: Yes, because the gross limit takes priority.
No. The axle limit must also be met.
Yes, if another axle is under its limit by the same amount.
questions.explanation: Gross and axle limits are separate checks. Rework the load and verify the weights before moving.

evidence.rationale: Gross and axle limits are separate checks. Rework the load and verify the weights before moving.
evidence.scope: A separately applicable axle limit has been exceeded.

questions.question: A route has a signed overhead restriction below the height of your loaded truck. What should you do?
options: Continue if the unloaded truck fits beneath the restriction.
Use a route with adequate clearance.
Approach slowly and see whether the load clears.
questions.explanation: Compare the restriction with the vehicle’s height as loaded. Use a route with sufficient clearance.

evidence.section: Section 6, Railway bridges and overhead structures
evidence.rationale: Compare the restriction with the vehicle’s height as loaded. Use a route with sufficient clearance.
evidence.scope: Signed overhead restriction lower than the actual loaded height.

questions.question: An abnormal indivisible load requires a Garda permit on the designated route and will then travel over local roads. What should the operator check before the move?
options: Whether the Garda permit removes all local-road requirements.
Whether a second driver can take over and bypass permit requirements.
Whether the local-road sections also need the relevant local authority permits.
questions.explanation: The RSA distinguishes designated routes covered by the Garda permit from roads requiring local authority permits.

evidence.section: Frequently asked questions, abnormal loads on designated and local roads
evidence.rationale: The RSA distinguishes designated routes covered by the Garda permit from roads requiring local authority permits.
evidence.scope: Abnormal indivisible load travelling over designated and local roads.

questions.question: Your vehicle has broken down on a motorway. Should you walk back along the shoulder to place a warning triangle?
options: No. The RSA advises against placing a triangle on a motorway.
Yes, if you wear a high-visibility vest.
Yes, whenever the triangle is carried as required equipment.
questions.explanation: Walking back to place the triangle exposes you to motorway traffic. Follow motorway breakdown procedures.

evidence.section: Section 11, What to do if your vehicle breaks down
evidence.rationale: Walking back to place the triangle exposes you to motorway traffic. Follow motorway breakdown procedures.
evidence.scope: Motorway breakdown, irrespective of whether the vehicle carries a triangle.

questions.question: An ambulance using its siren is behind you at a red signal. There is no safe movement available and nobody is directing you through. What should you do?
options: Cross the red light because the ambulance gives you priority.
Remain behind the red light and make room only when you can do so safely and lawfully.
Reverse without checking so the ambulance can move alongside.
questions.explanation: The RSA says drivers should not break a red light to let an emergency vehicle pass unless directed by Gardaí or emergency personnel.

evidence.section: Section 12, What to do when an emergency service vehicle approaches
evidence.rationale: The RSA says drivers should not break a red light to let an emergency vehicle pass unless directed by Gardaí or emergency personnel.
evidence.scope: No applicable direction from Gardaí or emergency service personnel.

questions.question: A person is injured in a collision you are involved in. No Garda is at the scene. After arranging immediate help, where must the collision be reported?
options: Only to the operator at the end of the shift.
Only to the person’s insurer.
To the nearest Garda station.
questions.explanation: The RSA requires reporting an injury collision to the nearest Garda station when no Garda is at the scene.

evidence.section: Section 14, What drivers must do at an incident or in an emergency
evidence.rationale: The RSA requires reporting an injury collision to the nearest Garda station when no Garda is at the scene.
evidence.scope: Driver involved in an injury collision.

questions.question: You are stopped in a tunnel and there is a fire in another vehicle ahead. What should you do according to the RSA?
options: Drive forward past the burning vehicle if there is an open lane.
Switch off, leave your vehicle and use the nearest available emergency exit.
Stay in the vehicle with the engine running until the smoke clears.
questions.explanation: With a fire ahead, leave the vehicle and use an emergency exit, taking account of signs and the safest route.

evidence.rationale: With a fire ahead, leave the vehicle and use an emergency exit, taking account of signs and the safest route.
evidence.scope: Vehicle already stopped, fire ahead in the tunnel.

questions.question: You realise you have entered the motorway against traffic and can reach the hard shoulder. What should you do?
options: Make a U-turn using the live lanes as soon as a gap appears.
Reverse along the carriageway to the point where you entered.
Pull in and stop, call the Gardaí and wait in a safe place.
questions.explanation: The RSA advises stopping on the hard shoulder and calling 999 or 112 rather than attempting to turn around.

evidence.section: Section 11, On the motorway, wrong-way driving
evidence.rationale: The RSA advises stopping on the hard shoulder and calling 999 or 112 rather than attempting to turn around.
evidence.scope: Wrong-way motorway entry with reachable hard shoulder.

questions.question: You pulled in safely and the first emergency vehicle has passed. What should you check before rejoining traffic?
options: Whether you can follow closely behind the first emergency vehicle.
Whether another emergency vehicle is following and whether it is safe to move out.
Whether a vehicle behind has copied your signal.
questions.explanation: Emergency vehicles may be travelling in succession. Observe and signal before merging back.

evidence.section: Section 12, What to do when an emergency service vehicle approaches
evidence.rationale: Emergency vehicles may be travelling in succession. Observe and signal before merging back.
evidence.scope: Stopped safely to let emergency vehicles pass.

questions.question: For the EU drivers’ hours weekly limit, when does a new week normally begin?
options: At the start of the driver’s first shift after a weekly rest.
At 00:00 on Monday.
At 00:00 on Sunday.
questions.explanation: The regulation defines a fixed Monday-to-Sunday week for the weekly driving total.

evidence.rationale: The regulation defines a fixed Monday-to-Sunday week for the weekly driving total.
evidence.scope: Uses the statutory week. Weekly rest deadlines are a separate calculation.

questions.question: An in-scope driver starts after daily rest at 21:00 and works past midnight. Does midnight by itself start a new daily driving allowance?
options: Yes, because the calendar date changes.
No. Daily driving is accumulated between the relevant rest periods.
Yes, provided the driver changes vehicles after midnight.
questions.explanation: The daily driving total follows the rest periods that define the day, not the calendar boundary.

evidence.rationale: The daily driving total follows the rest periods that define the day, not the calendar boundary.
evidence.scope: No new daily or weekly rest has started at midnight.

questions.question: A driver’s weekly rest ended at 06:00 on Monday. With no derogation, what is the latest time to start the next weekly rest?
options: 06:00 on the following Monday.
06:00 on Sunday.
Midnight on Sunday night.
questions.explanation: The next weekly rest must begin by the end of six consecutive 24-hour periods from the previous weekly rest’s end.

evidence.rationale: The next weekly rest must begin by the end of six consecutive 24-hour periods from the previous weekly rest’s end.
evidence.scope: Standard timing rule. Other limits may require an earlier start.

questions.question: An in-scope driver takes a permitted 32-hour reduced weekly rest. How much additional rest is owed for that reduction?
options: 8 hours.
13 hours.
24 hours.
questions.explanation: Compare the reduced rest with the 45-hour regular weekly minimum. The difference is 13 hours.

evidence.rationale: Compare the reduced rest with the 45-hour regular weekly minimum. The difference is 13 hours.
evidence.scope: A lawful single reduction. Compensation timing and attachment rules also apply.

questions.question: A driver is arranging the compensation owed for a reduced weekly rest. What kind of rest must it be attached to?
options: Any 45-minute break during the driving day.
Another rest period of at least nine hours.
Any period of availability longer than nine hours.
questions.explanation: Compensatory rest must be attached to another rest of at least nine hours.

evidence.rationale: Compensatory rest must be attached to another rest of at least nine hours.
evidence.scope: Standard EU rule. The compensation must also be taken in one block by the applicable deadline.

questions.question: For standard multi-manning, when can the first driver be alone at the start of the relevant driving period?
options: Until the first 45-minute break.
For up to half of the driving period.
During the first hour only.
questions.explanation: The second driver’s presence is optional in the first hour and required for the rest of the multi-manning period.

evidence.rationale: The second driver’s presence is optional in the first hour and required for the rest of the multi-manning period.
evidence.scope: Both drivers otherwise satisfy the conditions for multi-manning.

questions.question: You are the second driver in a moving vehicle and want the next 45 minutes to count as your break. What must you avoid?
options: Assisting the driver who is driving.
Remaining in the cab while the vehicle moves.
Taking the break until the vehicle is back at its base.
questions.explanation: A multi-manning break can be taken in the moving vehicle if the resting driver does not assist the driver at the wheel.

evidence.rationale: A multi-manning break can be taken in the moving vehicle if the resting driver does not assist the driver at the wheel.
evidence.scope: An in-scope multi-manned journey. The break must meet other applicable conditions.

questions.question: A truck driver accompanies the vehicle on a ferry and has an appropriate bunk. They are taking regular daily rest under the ferry provision. What is the interruption limit?
options: No more than two interruptions of up to one hour each.
Any number of interruptions provided the total is no more than one hour.
No more than two interruptions totalling no more than one hour.
questions.explanation: Both limits apply: at most two interruptions and a combined total of no more than one hour.

evidence.rationale: Both limits apply: at most two interruptions and a combined total of no more than one hour.
evidence.scope: Regular daily rest under the accompanied ferry provision. Other conditions still apply.

questions.question: You drive a car outside the regulation’s scope to collect an in-scope truck parked away from home and away from your normal base. How is the car journey classified?
options: Daily rest.
A driving break.
Other work.
questions.explanation: Driving an out-of-scope vehicle to take over the in-scope vehicle at a remote location counts as other work.

evidence.rationale: Driving an out-of-scope vehicle to take over the in-scope vehicle at a remote location counts as other work.
evidence.scope: The driver personally drives to a location that is neither home nor their normal operational centre.

questions.question: Your digital tachograph driver card has stopped working. Within what period must you apply for its replacement?
options: Seven working days.
Seven calendar days.
Fifteen calendar days.
questions.explanation: Apply within seven calendar days to the competent authority in your normal country of residence.

evidence.rationale: Apply within seven calendar days to the competent authority in your normal country of residence.
evidence.scope: Damaged, malfunctioning, lost or stolen card. Separate recording duties apply.

questions.question: Your tachograph driver card is stolen while working in another Member State. Where must you formally declare the theft?
options: To the competent authorities in the state where it was stolen.
Only to the authority in the state that issued the card.
Only to the vehicle operator in Ireland.
questions.explanation: The theft declaration is made in the state where the theft occurred. The replacement application is a separate step.

evidence.rationale: The theft declaration is made in the state where the theft occurred. The replacement application is a separate step.
evidence.scope: The card was stolen. Lost cards follow a different declaration rule.

questions.question: At a roadside check in a digital-tachograph vehicle, what time window applies to any manual records and printouts made by the driver?
options: Today and the preceding 28 days.
Today and the preceding 56 days.
Only the current calendar week.
questions.explanation: The current digital-tachograph inspection window includes the day of the check and the previous 56 days for such records.

evidence.rationale: The current digital-tachograph inspection window includes the day of the check and the previous 56 days for such records.
evidence.scope: Any manual records and printouts made in that period. Other records may also be required.

questions.question: You carry out other work away from a vehicle and therefore cannot enter it at the digital tachograph when it occurs. What should you do when recording the period?
options: Leave it blank because it happened outside the cab.
Enter it as driving because it happened during a shift.
Enter the period on the driver card using the tachograph’s manual entry facility.
questions.explanation: The manual input facility is used to capture qualifying activity that could not be recorded at the time.

evidence.rationale: The manual input facility is used to capture qualifying activity that could not be recorded at the time.
evidence.scope: Digital tachograph and an in-scope driver recording other work.

questions.question: When should you start using your driver card on a day when you drive a vehicle fitted with a digital tachograph?

From the moment you take over the vehicle.

As cosmetic damage that never needs reporting.
As a load-securing fault to be fixed with a lashing strap.

Treat it as normal whenever the vehicle is unloaded.
Report the pressure loss and have it investigated before use.

evidence.rationale: The check includes air leaks and pressure drop. An abnormal loss may affect systems that rely on compressed air.

questions.question: You are reviewing a direct-lashing design. Which strap rating does the HSA identify as the relevant one for deciding the required restraints?
options: Lashing capacity.
Standard hand force.
Breaking force.

Standard tension force.
The breaking force of the complete assembly.

options: Remove it from use and use a serviceable restraint.

Use it with lower tension if a second strap is present.

No. Use suitable, rated lashing points and follow the securing plan.

questions.question: Why does a stack of round timber need a restraint system that accounts for movement within the load?

Timber always slides as one solid mass, so internal movement cannot occur.

Report the strike immediately using the bridge’s emergency contact and identification details.
Finish the delivery and check again on your return.

evidence.rationale: Report the strike immediately even without visible damage. Give Iarnród Éireann the bridge identification number and what happened. If you cannot reach them immediately, notify An Garda Síochána straight away.

questions.question: On a road with an 80 km/h speed limit you are deciding whether there is enough room to pass a cyclist. What minimum clearance does the RSA recommend in that speed zone?

At least 1.5 metres.
At least half a metre.

evidence.rationale: The RSA recommends at least 1.5 metres where the speed limit exceeds 50 km/h. Wait if a safe pass is not possible.
evidence.scope: A recommendation for a speed zone above 50 km/h. Allow more space when circumstances require it.

questions.question: You want to pass a slow vehicle on a road where a dip hides part of the oncoming lane. When should you start the overtake?

Start as soon as you reach a broken centre line.
Start if a vehicle ahead has just overtaken successfully.

evidence.rationale: A dip can conceal oncoming traffic. A broken line alone does not establish that the manoeuvre is safe.
evidence.scope: Ordinary two-way road with a dip obscuring the road ahead.

questions.question: A cyclist moves towards the middle of the lane before a junction where visibility is poor. What might they be doing?
options: Giving following vehicles a signal to pass immediately.
Showing that they are about to stop cycling.
Improving their view and making themselves easier for others to see.
questions.explanation: The RSA notes that cyclists may use a more central position to see and be seen near hazards.

evidence.section: Section 5, Sharing the road with cyclists
evidence.rationale: The RSA notes that cyclists may use a more central position to see and be seen near hazards.
evidence.scope: A cyclist taking a more visible position near a junction.

questions.question: A vehicle normally prohibited from using the outside motorway lane cannot proceed in the inner lane because of an obstruction. What exception does the RSA describe?
options: It may use the outside lane whenever an inner lane is moving more slowly.
It must always stop until the obstruction is removed, even if directed around it.
It may use the outside lane to get past the obstruction when safe.
questions.explanation: The exception is for an obstruction that prevents progress in the inner lane. It is different from normal overtaking.

evidence.section: Section 11, Using lanes properly, outside-lane exceptions
evidence.rationale: The exception is for an obstruction that prevents progress in the inner lane. It is different from normal overtaking.
evidence.scope: Applicable vehicle restriction and a genuine obstruction. Follow site directions and signs.

questions.question: An orange diamond sign ahead has a black symbol of a worker digging. What does it warn you about?
options: The end of a detour.
A school crossing ahead.
Roadworks ahead.
questions.explanation: Orange warning signs are used for roadworks. This symbol alerts drivers to work ahead so they can adapt early.

evidence.rationale: Orange warning signs are used for roadworks. This symbol alerts drivers to work ahead so they can adapt early.
evidence.scope: Standard roadwork warning sign.

questions.question: You approach a red traffic light and there is no stop line. Where does the RSA say you must stop?
options: Before the traffic light.
Past the light if the first crossing is clear.
At the far side of the junction.

evidence.rationale: Where no stop line is provided, the red signal still prohibits proceeding beyond the light.
evidence.scope: Steady red, no stop line and no direction overriding the signal.

questions.question: What does the yellow diamond with a black winding arrow warn about?
options: A mandatory U-turn ahead.
A one-way lane that ends ahead.
A series of dangerous bends ahead.

evidence.rationale: The winding arrow on a yellow warning diamond signals a series of bends requiring care.
evidence.scope: The standard warning sign for a series of dangerous bends.

questions.question: A passenger has boarded and is still paying at the ticket machine beside the driver. What should happen before moving off?

Begin pulling away and finish taking payment in motion.
Signal left while continuing the transaction and then move without another check.

evidence.rationale: The RSA advises completing customer transactions before moving the bus.
evidence.scope: Ordinary passenger service at a stop.

questions.question: You are at a safe hail-and-ride stopping point on a two-way road. It is not a designated bus stop. Which side should you use for routine boarding?
options: The nearside, away from opposing traffic.
The offside so passengers can be seen by oncoming drivers.
Whichever side leaves the driver closer to the centre line.

questions.question: A coach driver wants to make a non-urgent announcement using a hand-operated public address system. When should they use it?
options: When the coach is stationary.
When the coach is moving slowly in a queue.
Any time there are no pedestrians nearby.

evidence.rationale: The RSA advises drivers to use hand-operated public address equipment while stationary.
evidence.scope: Hand-operated system used by the driver, routine announcement.

questions.question: You have time to adjust speed before a bend on a low-grip road. Which action makes a skid more likely?

A sudden, hard brake application.
Taking account of the road surface before choosing speed.

questions.question: A road is posted at 80 km/h, but the category of vehicle you are driving has a lower applicable limit. Which upper limit controls?
options: The lower limit for the vehicle.
The posted 80 km/h limit because it is on a sign.
An average of the two limits.

The reversing camera display.
The tunnel signs and radio announcements from the operator.

Stow them safely as the procedure specifies.

Wedge it against an air line to hold it in place.
Stow it securely in its intended position.

questions.question: Your lane shows a red X on an overhead lane-control sign. The pavement beyond looks clear. What does the signal require?

Continue below the last posted speed limit.

Move to the right-hand lane when you can change lanes safely.

evidence.rationale: A sideways arrow directs drivers to the lane it points towards. Make the lane change safely.
evidence.scope: An overhead directional lane-control signal, not a downward arrow or junction filter.

questions.question: At a red light there are two white stop lines with a cycle waiting area between them. Which line should a truck stop behind on approach?

Either line if no cyclist is waiting.
