evidence.rationale: Motor traffic waits behind the first line so the cycle area remains available.

Yes, as long as the traffic lights for the railway are unlit.

evidence.rationale: A yield line requires giving way. Whether you need to stop depends on the traffic and visibility.
evidence.scope: A yield line with a clear view and no conflicting traffic.

questions.question: The gaps between the broken white centre lines become shorter as you approach a bend. What is the purpose of this change?

questions.question: A street has a No Entry sign with an Except Trams and Access plate. You have no delivery or other access need on the street. May you use it as a shortcut?

No. The access exception does not cover a through journey.

questions.question: The children have finished crossing and the school warden lowers the sign, but the warden is still in the road. When can you move?

After the warden has safely returned to the footpath and the road is clear.

questions.question: A warning begins while your vehicle is already on an automatic railway crossing, and the exit is clear. What should you do?

Reverse back onto the approach road.
Move clear promptly.

evidence.section: Section 6, Automated railway level crossings with barriers and flashing red lights, page 98
evidence.rationale: Once already on the crossing with a clear exit, move off the tracks as quickly as safely possible.
evidence.scope: Vehicle already on the crossing with the exit clear.

questions.question: A with-flow bus lane’s plate shows it is reserved from 07:00 to 10:00. At 08:30, may a goods vehicle use it to bypass a queue?

No. Stay in a lane available to goods vehicles.

questions.question: A vehicle begins a legal overtake on a two-way road. It remains safe for you to maintain your current speed. What should you do?

questions.question: A driver ahead has moved out and signalled right. You are continuing straight and can pass on the left safely and legally. What does the RSA allow?

Passing only on the right, even across the driver’s intended turn.
Using the footpath to leave extra room.

questions.question: A vehicle slows on the approach to a zebra crossing. You cannot yet see the far side of it. May you overtake before the crossing?

Yes, if the stripes are clear on your side.

evidence.rationale: Overtaking at or near a pedestrian crossing can hide a person from view and is prohibited.

questions.question: Conditions are good and there is room in the motorway exit lane. Where should you normally start reducing speed for the slip road?

Well before the exit while still in the main traffic lane, regardless of conditions.
Only after completing the bend on the slip road.

questions.question: You want to park three metres from a road junction. No parking spaces are marked there. May you park in that position?

Yes, if the vehicle does not cover a yellow line.

evidence.scope: Ordinary parking without a marked bay or other applicable exception.

questions.question: A roadside parking space looks too narrow, so a driver considers putting two wheels on the footpath. What should they do?

Find a lawful place where the whole vehicle fits without using the footpath.
Use the footpath if the vehicle is within sight of the driver.
questions.explanation: Parking partly on a footpath obstructs the space intended for pedestrians and is prohibited.

evidence.rationale: Parking partly on a footpath obstructs the space intended for pedestrians and is prohibited.
evidence.scope: Ordinary public-road parking.

questions.question: You are in a goods vehicle and arrive at a signed loading bay 25 minutes before the collection team is ready. May you use the bay as a waiting space?
options: No. The bay is reserved for actual loading or unloading.
Yes. A goods vehicle can use it for any purpose for up to 30 minutes.
Yes, as long as the driver stays in the cab.
questions.explanation: The restriction concerns the activity as well as the vehicle. Use a loading bay only for loading or unloading within its applicable time limit.

evidence.section: Section 10, No parking, loading bays, page 144
evidence.rationale: The restriction concerns the activity as well as the vehicle. Use a loading bay only for loading or unloading within its applicable time limit.
evidence.scope: A signed ordinary loading bay, with no loading or unloading taking place.

questions.question: While driving, your dispatcher sends a routine message. How should you deal with it?
options: Wait until you are safely and legally parked before reading it.
Read it when stopped briefly in a moving queue.
Read it while holding the phone low in the cab.
questions.explanation: The RSA prohibits reading phone messages while driving. A routine dispatch message is not an emergency.

evidence.rationale: The RSA prohibits reading phone messages while driving. A routine dispatch message is not an emergency.
evidence.scope: Routine non-emergency message and no need to handle the phone while driving.

questions.question: You are approaching a junction to turn left. A cyclist ahead near the kerb may be going straight. What is the safest approach?
options: Pass the cyclist just before turning so they can see your indicator.
Move left early to prevent the cyclist continuing straight.
Stay behind and turn only when the cyclist’s path is clear.
questions.explanation: Avoid overtaking a cyclist just before you turn left. They may continue straight across your intended path.

evidence.rationale: Avoid overtaking a cyclist just before you turn left. They may continue straight across your intended path.
evidence.scope: Cyclist near the kerb approaching the same junction.

questions.question: After parking legally, you need to open the driver’s door towards moving traffic. What should you check first?
options: Open it slightly first to warn anyone approaching.
Check only the pavement because your vehicle is stationary.
Look for cyclists and others passing and give them space before opening the door.
questions.explanation: Use the mirrors and check the area beside the door. An opening door can obstruct a passing cyclist.

evidence.section: Section 19, Cycle tracks and parking, page 225
evidence.rationale: Use the mirrors and check the area beside the door. An opening door can obstruct a passing cyclist.
evidence.scope: Door opens towards traffic after a legal stop.

questions.question: You enter an area where pedestrians, cyclists and vehicles share the same low-speed space. How should you drive there?
options: At the speed used on the main road immediately before it.
Very slowly, allowing time to react to people sharing the space.
At a steady speed so pedestrians can predict your path, even when people are close.
questions.explanation: Shared spaces call for very low speed because people and vehicles can use the same area.

evidence.rationale: Shared spaces call for very low speed because people and vehicles can use the same area.
evidence.scope: A designated shared space.

questions.question: At midnight in a built-up area, a colleague suggests sounding the horn to let a depot worker know you have arrived. There is no traffic emergency. What should you do?
options: Give one short blast because you are driving a work vehicle.
Use another way to contact them.
Sound the horn if the depot worker has asked you to do so.
questions.explanation: The RSA prohibits using the horn in a built-up area from 23:30 to 07:00 unless there is a traffic emergency.

evidence.rationale: The RSA prohibits using the horn in a built-up area from 23:30 to 07:00 unless there is a traffic emergency.
evidence.scope: Midnight in a built-up area, no emergency.

questions.question: Why should a driver have misaligned headlights adjusted even if both lights work?
options: Poor aim affects only the dashboard brightness.
Misalignment only matters if one bulb is completely out.
Poor aim can reduce the useful light on the road and dazzle others.
questions.explanation: A working headlamp must also aim correctly to light the road without excessive glare.

evidence.rationale: A working headlamp must also aim correctly to light the road without excessive glare.
evidence.scope: Headlights function but are misaligned.

questions.question: On an unlit road at night you catch up with another vehicle. Which headlights should you normally use while following?
options: Main beam so the driver ahead can see farther.
Dipped headlights.
Sidelights alone to prevent mirror glare.
questions.explanation: Dipped headlights help avoid dazzling the driver ahead through their mirrors.

evidence.section: Section 5, When to use headlights, page 64
evidence.rationale: Dipped headlights help avoid dazzling the driver ahead through their mirrors.
evidence.scope: Ordinary night driving while following another vehicle.

questions.question: You are stopping in a queue where emergency vehicles may need to get through. What can you do before one arrives to preserve room to move?
options: Stop as close as possible to the vehicle ahead.
Stop partly in the adjacent lane to keep it empty.
Leave manoeuvring space in front when stopping.
questions.explanation: Leaving some space when stopped gives you room to move safely if an emergency vehicle needs to pass.

evidence.section: Section 12, What to do when an emergency service vehicle approaches, page 171
evidence.rationale: Leaving some space when stopped gives you room to move safely if an emergency vehicle needs to pass.
evidence.scope: Ordinary stopped traffic. Follow directions and move only if safe.

questions.question: You are approaching a person controlling an animal on the road. What is the safest way to prepare to pass?
options: Use the horn to make the animal move aside.
Slow down, allow plenty of room and be ready to stop.
Pass at normal speed before the animal can move.
questions.explanation: Animals may react unpredictably. Approach slowly and give the person room to control the animal.

evidence.rationale: Animals may react unpredictably. Approach slowly and give the person room to control the animal.
evidence.scope: Ordinary approach to animal traffic. Avoid startling animals.

questions.question: Your vehicle stalls on railway tracks at a level crossing. What should you do first?
options: Keep everyone in the vehicle while trying to restart it.
Ask a passenger to stand on the track and signal approaching trains.
Get everyone well clear of the railway.
questions.explanation: People should move well clear of the railway. Then contact the railway controller using the crossing information.

evidence.section: Section 6, Emergency actions at level crossings, page 92
evidence.rationale: People should move well clear of the railway. Then contact the railway controller using the crossing information.
evidence.scope: Vehicle stalled on railway tracks.

questions.question: You see an object obstructing traffic on a motorway. You have passed it and can report it from a safe location. What does the RSA advise?
options: Return on foot along the shoulder and move it yourself.
Wait to report it until you see a vehicle strike it.
Tell the Gardaí and leave removal to those who can manage it safely.
questions.explanation: The RSA advises reporting motorway obstructions and warns drivers against trying to remove them themselves.

evidence.rationale: The RSA advises reporting motorway obstructions and warns drivers against trying to remove them themselves.
evidence.scope: Road user reporting an obstruction from a safe place.

questions.question: A fire has started in another vehicle behind you in a tunnel. The road ahead is clear and the operator has issued no contrary instructions. What should you do?
options: Continue out of the tunnel safely.
Reverse towards the fire to warn the other driver.
Stop in your lane and wait for the fire to reach you.
questions.explanation: The RSA advises driving out if the fire is behind you. Conditions and instructions still determine whether the route ahead is safe.

evidence.section: Section 11, Fire in another vehicle, page 164
evidence.rationale: The RSA advises driving out if the fire is behind you. Conditions and instructions still determine whether the route ahead is safe.
evidence.scope: Fire behind the driver with a usable route ahead.

questions.question: You are moving an unusually long, low vehicle over a minor-road level crossing protected by lights only. What should you arrange before crossing?
options: Contact the railway using the crossing information to obtain permission.
Proceed whenever a smaller vehicle crosses immediately ahead.
Wait for a regular train to pass and then cross without contacting anyone.
questions.explanation: The RSA calls for contacting the railway before unusual vehicle movements at the specified crossing types.

evidence.section: Section 6, Unusual movements across level crossings, page 92
evidence.rationale: The RSA calls for contacting the railway before unusual vehicle movements at the specified crossing types.
evidence.scope: An awkward vehicle at a minor-road crossing protected by traffic lights only.

questions.question: An HGV tyre has a deep cut with signs of carcass damage, but it is still holding air. How should you treat it?
options: Use it at a lower speed if the pressure holds.
Put the damaged tyre on a different axle and drive.
Keep the truck out of service and report it for qualified assessment.
questions.explanation: A tyre can be unsafe despite holding air. Deep cuts and carcass damage are part of the roadworthiness check.

evidence.section: Section 6, External vehicle checks, tyres, page 44
evidence.rationale: A tyre can be unsafe despite holding air. Deep cuts and carcass damage are part of the roadworthiness check.
evidence.scope: Deep cut with signs of structural tyre damage.

questions.question: On a familiar truck, a dashboard gauge gives no reading when it would normally be active. What should you do before use?
options: Rely on the last value recorded by the previous driver.
Drive if none of the exterior lamps are affected.
Record and report the fault so it can be assessed.
questions.explanation: Instruments and warning devices are included in the HGV check. A missing reading should be investigated.

evidence.section: Walk-around check items, Instruments, gauges and warning devices
evidence.rationale: Instruments and warning devices are included in the HGV check. A missing reading should be investigated.
evidence.scope: An active instrument fails its normal function check.

questions.question: Before departure you see a fresh patch beneath the truck that appears to be fuel or oil. What should you do?
options: Assume it was left by the last vehicle to park there and continue.
Drive to warm the vehicle and see whether the patch disappears.
Check and report the suspected leak before taking the vehicle out.
questions.explanation: The HGV checklist includes fuel and oil leaks. Have a suspected leak assessed under the operator’s procedure.

evidence.rationale: The HGV checklist includes fuel and oil leaks. Have a suspected leak assessed under the operator’s procedure.
evidence.scope: Fresh fluid of uncertain origin noticed during a pre-use check.

questions.question: The driver’s seat belt will not latch during a pre-use check. What is appropriate?
options: Keep the webbing across your lap without latching it.
Report the defect and have it addressed before driving.
Drive if the seat itself is correctly adjusted.
questions.explanation: The seat belt is a distinct safety item. A failed latch prevents the belt working as intended.

evidence.section: Walk-around check items, Driver’s seat and seat belts
evidence.rationale: The seat belt is a distinct safety item. A failed latch prevents the belt working as intended.
evidence.scope: The driver’s fitted seat belt cannot be fastened.

questions.question: Road dirt obscures an HGV’s rear reflectors, although its tail lights work. What should you do before departure?
options: Leave the reflectors because the lamps are working.
Switch on rear fog lights to compensate.
Clean the reflectors and confirm they are visible.
questions.explanation: Reflectors are a separate visibility check. Keep them clean so they can return light from other vehicles.

evidence.rationale: Reflectors are a separate visibility check. Keep them clean so they can return light from other vehicles.
evidence.scope: Working tail lights and dirt-obscured reflectors.

questions.question: You find a damaged spray-suppression flap during your HGV check. Should you ignore it because the road is dry?
options: No. Record and report it as a defect for assessment.
Yes, unless it is raining at the time of the check.
Yes, as long as the rear lights are still visible.
questions.explanation: The checklist includes spray-suppression equipment. Current weather does not remove the need to record a defect.

evidence.rationale: The checklist includes spray-suppression equipment. Current weather does not remove the need to record a defect.
evidence.scope: HGV equipped with a spray-suppression flap.

questions.question: A rear plate is hidden by road grime after a previous shift. What should you do before the next journey?
options: Write the registration on a note in the cab instead.
Clean it at the next annual vehicle test.
Clean the plate so its characters can be read.
questions.explanation: Number and marker plates are part of the HGV check. A plate needs to be legible from outside the vehicle.

evidence.section: Walk-around check items, Number plates and marker plates
evidence.rationale: Number and marker plates are part of the HGV check. A plate needs to be legible from outside the vehicle.
evidence.scope: A fitted rear number plate is obscured by dirt.

questions.question: Your load plan permits two kinds of boxes to be stacked and the lower boxes can support the load. Where should the heavier boxes go to improve stability?
options: At the top so they press down on the lighter boxes.
Lower in the stack, with the weight suitably distributed.
Alternating at the top corners to equalise the height.
questions.explanation: Putting heavier items lower helps keep the centre of gravity down. Check the weight and strength of the complete stack.

evidence.rationale: Putting heavier items lower helps keep the centre of gravity down. Check the weight and strength of the complete stack.
evidence.scope: Stackable cargo with suitable supporting packaging and a securing plan.

questions.question: After taking part of a multi-drop load off a vehicle, what should the driver check before continuing?
options: Only that the gross weight has fallen.
How the remaining weight is distributed and how the remaining load is secured.
Only that the doors can be closed without touching the goods.
questions.explanation: Removing cargo changes the loading pattern and can affect axle weights, stability and the remaining restraint.

evidence.rationale: Removing cargo changes the loading pattern and can affect axle weights, stability and the remaining restraint.
evidence.scope: A partial delivery changes the original load arrangement.

questions.question: A conventional ISO freight container is placed on a compatible skeletal trailer. Which fittings provide positive restraint through the container’s corner castings?
options: The ordinary curtain buckles.
The trailer’s serviceable twist locks.
The air lines between tractor and trailer.
questions.explanation: The twist locks engage the container’s corner castings. The operator must confirm the fitted system is correctly engaged before transport.

evidence.rationale: The twist locks engage the container’s corner castings. The operator must confirm the fitted system is correctly engaged before transport.
evidence.scope: Compatible container and skeletal trailer designed for twist-lock restraint.

questions.question: Why can a partially filled bulk liquid container affect a truck’s stability when it changes direction?
options: The liquid can move inside the container and shift the load’s effect on the vehicle.
Part filling always locks the liquid in place.
Direction changes affect the container only when it is empty.
questions.explanation: A liquid load can surge inside a partly filled container. The effect is relevant when choosing how to drive and carry it.

evidence.rationale: A liquid load can surge inside a partly filled container. The effect is relevant when choosing how to drive and carry it.
evidence.scope: Partially filled bulk liquid container.

questions.question: A webbing lashing in an approved securing plan passes over an edge that could damage it. What should the driver check?
options: That appropriate edge protection is fitted before tensioning it.
That the lashing is twisted so the edge cannot be seen.
That the strap has a high breaking force, which makes edge protection unnecessary.
questions.explanation: Use suitable edge protection to protect the webbing and distribute the tie-down force.

evidence.rationale: Use suitable edge protection to protect the webbing and distribute the tie-down force.
evidence.scope: Webbing contacts an edge. Use equipment compatible with the securing plan.

questions.question: You heard a click during fifth-wheel coupling. What further check does the cited procedure describe to verify engagement?
options: A controlled low-gear pull check against the secured trailer, following the operator’s procedure.
Move straight onto the road because the click verifies the lock.
Release the trailer brake and lift the trailer with the landing gear to test it.
questions.explanation: The procedure uses a controlled pull to help check that the locking mechanism has engaged. Complete all other locking and visual checks.

evidence.rationale: The procedure uses a controlled pull to help check that the locking mechanism has engaged. Complete all other locking and visual checks.
evidence.scope: Conventional fifth wheel. The vehicle’s approved safe procedure governs the sequence.

questions.question: You need to leave a semi-trailer temporarily. What should you decide before beginning uncoupling?
options: Whether other vehicles are likely to hear the air lines disconnect.
Whether the tractor can leave before the trailer brakes are applied.
Whether there is a safe and legal place to park and support it.
questions.explanation: The uncoupling procedure starts by selecting a safe, legal parking position. Trailer support and movement must be controlled.

evidence.rationale: The uncoupling procedure starts by selecting a safe, legal parking position. Trailer support and movement must be controlled.
evidence.scope: Choose the site before uncoupling. Follow the operator’s full procedure.

questions.question: The trailer is mechanically coupled and its lights work. Which separate connection check still relates to the trailer braking system?
options: Check that the trailer brake connections are correct and secure.
Check the lighting connector twice in place of the brake check.
Check only that the trailer number plate is fitted.
questions.explanation: Electrical lighting and trailer brake connections are separate pre-use checks.

evidence.section: Walk-around check items, Trailer Brake Connections
evidence.rationale: Electrical lighting and trailer brake connections are separate pre-use checks.
evidence.scope: A coupled trailer with separate brake and lighting connections.

questions.question: On a long descent, why may an appropriate retarder be useful in a truck?
options: It provides more grip at the tyres regardless of conditions.
It replaces the need to select an appropriate speed before descending.
It can help control speed while reducing reliance on the wheel brakes.
questions.explanation: Endurance braking can control speed through the driveline so that less continuous use of the service brakes is needed.

evidence.rationale: Endurance braking can control speed through the driveline so that less continuous use of the service brakes is needed.
evidence.scope: A truck fitted with a retarder. Use it according to the vehicle procedure and conditions.

questions.question: A wheel is about to lock during braking on a slippery road. What is the principal benefit of the truck’s working ABS?
options: It helps preserve steering control by limiting wheel lock.
It guarantees a shorter stopping distance in every condition.
It increases the available grip between the tyre and the road.
questions.explanation: ABS changes brake pressure to reduce wheel lock and help the driver retain steering. It does not guarantee a shorter stop.

evidence.rationale: ABS changes brake pressure to reduce wheel lock and help the driver retain steering. It does not guarantee a shorter stop.
evidence.scope: Vehicle with working ABS. Use the manufacturer’s braking instructions.

questions.question: A front tyre blows on a straight road and you have clear space ahead. What immediate response does the RSA advise?
options: Apply the foot brake as hard as possible before correcting the steering.
Hold the steering wheel firmly, ease off the accelerator and avoid harsh braking.
Accelerate until the steering feels lighter.
questions.explanation: A front blowout can pull the vehicle sideways. Steer firmly and allow speed to reduce when space permits.

evidence.section: If your vehicle suffers a tyre blowout
evidence.rationale: A front blowout can pull the vehicle sideways. Steer firmly and allow speed to reduce when space permits.
evidence.scope: Front tyre blowout with space ahead. Respond to the immediate road situation.

questions.question: After safely crossing an unattended gated level crossing, what should you do about the gates?
options: Leave them open for the next road user.
Shut and fasten them after you.
Close only the gate on the side from which you approached.
questions.explanation: The RSA directs users to shut and fasten the gates after crossing. Open gates can expose others to the railway.

evidence.rationale: The RSA directs users to shut and fasten the gates after crossing. Open gates can expose others to the railway.
evidence.scope: User-worked, unattended level crossing with gates.

questions.question: The width of your vehicle exceeds the number on a signed maximum-width restriction. Can you proceed if the road ahead has no oncoming traffic?
options: Yes, as long as you keep to the middle of the road.
No. Find a route that meets the signed width restriction.
Yes, if you fold a mirror in and drive slowly past the sign.
questions.explanation: The width limit applies even when other traffic is absent. Plan a suitable alternative.

evidence.section: Section 6, Upright signs, maximum width, page 69
evidence.rationale: The width limit applies even when other traffic is absent. Plan a suitable alternative.
evidence.scope: Vehicle exceeds the dimension to which the signed restriction applies.

questions.question: What makes an over-limit load indivisible in the RSA’s abnormal-load guidance?
options: The load cannot be divided into smaller loads.
The load has been placed on a single trailer.
The customer prefers it to arrive in one delivery.
questions.explanation: The indivisible element concerns whether the load itself can be divided. The abnormal element concerns exceeding a relevant limit.

evidence.section: Frequently asked questions, What is an abnormal indivisible load?
evidence.rationale: The indivisible element concerns whether the load itself can be divided. The abnormal element concerns exceeding a relevant limit.
evidence.scope: Use the RSA guidance to determine what permits apply to the actual move.

questions.question: A non-agricultural indivisible load exceeds the ordinary legal height limit. Which authority’s permit does the RSA table identify for excess height?
options: A Driver Theory Test Service permit.
A Garda designated-route permit for length and width alone.
A local authority permit.
questions.explanation: The RSA table directs over-height cases in this category to the local authority. Other excess dimensions can create additional requirements.

evidence.section: Frequently asked questions, How do I know which permit to apply for?
evidence.rationale: The RSA table directs over-height cases in this category to the local authority. Other excess dimensions can create additional requirements.
evidence.scope: Non-agricultural abnormal indivisible load exceeding the height limit.

questions.question: An in-scope driver uses a digital tachograph without automatic recording of the country data in question. Which country information is required for the daily working period?
options: The countries in which the daily working period begins and ends.
Only the country that issued the driver’s licence.
Only the country where the vehicle was registered.
questions.explanation: Country symbols identify where the daily work begins and ends. Automatic recording and border entries have separate provisions.

evidence.rationale: Country symbols identify where the daily work begins and ends. Automatic recording and border entries have separate provisions.
evidence.scope: Digital tachograph without the applicable automatic location recording.

questions.question: Your tachograph card malfunctions while you are away from home. Where should you return the malfunctioning card?
options: To the competent authority in your Member State of normal residence.
To the police in the country where you noticed the fault.
To the vehicle manufacturer.
questions.explanation: The return rule for a damaged or malfunctioning card uses normal residence. Theft and loss have separate declaration rules.

evidence.rationale: The return rule for a damaged or malfunctioning card uses normal residence. Theft and loss have separate declaration rules.
evidence.scope: Malfunctioning card, not a stolen or lost card.

questions.question: Under the standard EU two-week rule, what is the permitted minimum pattern if an in-scope goods driver takes one reduced weekly rest?
options: Two reduced weekly rests of 24 hours with no regular weekly rest.
One regular weekly rest and one reduced weekly rest of 15 hours.
One regular weekly rest and one reduced weekly rest of at least 24 hours.
questions.explanation: The standard pattern in two consecutive weeks permits one regular weekly rest and one reduced weekly rest of at least 24 hours.

evidence.rationale: The standard pattern in two consecutive weeks permits one regular weekly rest and one reduced weekly rest of at least 24 hours.
evidence.scope: No exception for qualifying international goods operations. Compensation and timing rules still apply.

questions.question: An in-scope solo goods driver finishes their previous rest at 05:00 on Tuesday. With no exception, by when must the required new daily rest have been taken?
options: By the end of Wednesday’s calendar day.
By 05:00 on Wednesday.
It only has to start by 05:00 on Wednesday.
questions.explanation: The required new daily rest must fall within the 24-hour period following the end of the previous daily or weekly rest.

evidence.rationale: The required new daily rest must fall within the 24-hour period following the end of the previous daily or weekly rest.
evidence.scope: Standard solo rule. The applicable rest length and any split are separate requirements.

questions.question: At night, a goods driver sees an empty contra-flow bus lane running opposite the traffic beside it. May they use it as a shortcut?
options: Yes. All bus lanes become general lanes after the evening peak.
No. The contra-flow lane is reserved and does not open to ordinary trucks at night.
Yes, if the truck uses its dipped headlights.
questions.explanation: A contra-flow bus lane is reserved in both daytime and night-time. A permitted cycling exception does not cover a goods vehicle.

evidence.rationale: A contra-flow bus lane is reserved in both daytime and night-time. A permitted cycling exception does not cover a goods vehicle.
evidence.scope: An ordinary goods vehicle without an authorised exemption.

questions.question: One continuous white line and one broken white line run together along the centre of a two-way road. The continuous line is nearest you. Which line applies to you?
options: The continuous line nearest your lane.
The broken line because it is visible beside the continuous one.
Whichever one gives the larger lane on approach.
questions.explanation: Drivers obey the line nearest them. A broken line on the other side does not cancel the nearer continuous line.

evidence.rationale: Drivers obey the line nearest them. A broken line on the other side does not cancel the nearer continuous line.
evidence.scope: Ordinary driving without an applicable exception to the continuous line.

questions.question: You have just finished a night shift and are planning a long drive after very little sleep. What is the safest change to the plan?
options: Keep the same plan but leave before traffic increases.
Drive faster in daylight so the journey takes less time.
Arrange to get adequate sleep before driving or use another safe means of travel.
questions.explanation: Sleep is the basis for managing fatigue, and driving after night work is a recognised risk.

evidence.section: Section 13, Driver tiredness and fatigue, page 176
evidence.rationale: Sleep is the basis for managing fatigue, and driving after night work is a recognised risk.
evidence.scope: Trip planning before setting off, not an immediate on-road response.

questions.question: A rigid goods vehicle has a maximum authorised mass above 3,500 kg and is travelling on a motorway signed at 120 km/h. It is towing nothing. What vehicle speed limit applies?
options: 80 km/h.
90 km/h.
questions.explanation: The motorway-specific vehicle limit for this goods vehicle is 90 km/h. A lower posted limit or conditions can require less.

evidence.section: Section 8, Speed limits for vehicles, pages 120–121
evidence.rationale: The motorway-specific vehicle limit for this goods vehicle is 90 km/h. A lower posted limit or conditions can require less.
evidence.scope: Ordinary rigid goods vehicle above 3,500 kg, motorway, no trailer and no lower limit.

questions.question: A driver holds only a learner permit for the vehicle they are driving. Can they use a motorway if a qualified accompanying driver is in the cab?
options: Yes. A qualified accompanying driver removes the motorway restriction.
No. A learner permit for that vehicle does not allow motorway driving.
Yes, if the learner stays in the left lane.
questions.explanation: Learner permit holders cannot drive on a motorway under the ordinary rules, even with an accompanying driver.

evidence.rationale: Learner permit holders cannot drive on a motorway under the ordinary rules, even with an accompanying driver.
evidence.scope: Driver holds a learner permit for the category and has no full entitlement for it.

questions.question: A vehicle behind dazzles you through a fitted interior mirror with a night-driving setting. What can help reduce the glare?
options: Turn the mirror away from the road and leave it there.
Switch your rear fog lights on to warn the following driver.
Use the mirror’s night-driving setting while retaining a rear view.
questions.explanation: The RSA advises using the interior mirror’s night setting when reflected glare comes from behind.

evidence.section: Section 5, What to do if you are dazzled, page 65
evidence.rationale: The RSA advises using the interior mirror’s night setting when reflected glare comes from behind.
evidence.scope: Vehicle fitted with an interior mirror and a night-driving setting.

questions.question: At a clear bus stop, you can pull in closer to the kerb safely. Why does that matter for boarding?
options: A larger gap gives passengers more time to see the bus.
A smaller gap makes it easier for passengers who have difficulty stepping across it.
The gap affects only the passengers’ view of the destination display.
questions.explanation: Stop suitably close to the kerb where practical to reduce the step across for passengers.

evidence.section: Section A, Hurrying loading/unloading passengers, p. 4
evidence.rationale: Stop suitably close to the kerb where practical to reduce the step across for passengers.
evidence.scope: A safe, clear stop where positioning nearer the kerb is possible.

questions.question: As you are about to close the doors, your mirror shows another passenger about to step into the entrance. What should you do?
options: Keep the doors open while it is safe and make sure boarding is complete before closing them.
Close the doors immediately if everyone already inside has paid.
Close the doors slowly so the boarding passenger can push them open.
questions.explanation: Use the door-area and blind-spot checks before closing. Do not close the doors on someone clearly about to board.

evidence.section: Section C, Boarding and alighting, p. 27
evidence.rationale: Use the door-area and blind-spot checks before closing. Do not close the doors on someone clearly about to board.
evidence.scope: Bus stationary at a safe, authorised stop.

questions.question: A person using a white cane is waiting at a stop you serve and may not see your destination display. How should you help them identify your service?
options: Wait for them to read the display before stopping.
Stop and tell them the service number and destination.
Tell a nearby passenger to point to the destination display.
questions.explanation: The RSA advises identifying the route and destination verbally to find out whether the person wants your service.

evidence.section: Section F, Passengers with impaired vision, p. 36
evidence.rationale: The RSA advises identifying the route and destination verbally to find out whether the person wants your service.
evidence.scope: Person at a stop on your route who may need the service identified.

questions.question: A passenger boards with a guide dog that is working. How should you interact with the dog?
options: Call the dog to your seat so the passenger can find the entrance.
Avoid distracting it. Speak directly to the passenger if they need help.
Offer it food while the passenger finds a seat.
questions.explanation: Distracting a working guide dog can interfere with the assistance it provides.

evidence.rationale: Distracting a working guide dog can interfere with the assistance it provides.
evidence.scope: Working guide dog accompanying a passenger.

questions.question: A passenger asks for the accessible ramp. You cannot see any obvious disability. How should you respond?
options: Refuse unless the passenger is using a wheelchair.
Use the ramp when safe and follow your vehicle’s procedure.
Wait for them to prove why they cannot use the step.
questions.explanation: A need for step-free access may be non-visible. RSA guidance says to use the ramp when requested.

evidence.rationale: A need for step-free access may be non-visible. RSA guidance says to use the ramp when requested.
evidence.scope: A passenger requests the ramp and the stop and equipment allow safe use.

questions.question: A TFI low-floor bus has a designated wheelchair space currently occupied by luggage. A wheelchair user needs it. What is the space’s priority use?
options: The first passenger to occupy the space keeps it throughout the journey.
The wheelchair user has priority. Ask for the luggage to be moved safely.
Use the aisle for the wheelchair so the luggage can stay in the space.
questions.explanation: TFI gives wheelchair users priority in the designated space. Keep the aisle and access route clear.

evidence.rationale: TFI gives wheelchair users priority in the designated space. Keep the aisle and access route clear.
evidence.scope: TFI low-floor service with a designated wheelchair space.

questions.question: A TFI bus is still kneeling and its ramp has not reached the footpath. When should the passenger start boarding via the ramp?
options: As soon as the driver activates the ramp switch.
After the vehicle and ramp have settled safely and the ramp rests on the footpath.
While the ramp is descending, if the passenger can reach it.
questions.explanation: The guidance asks passengers to keep clear during deployment and wait for the ramp to rest on the footpath.

evidence.rationale: The guidance asks passengers to keep clear during deployment and wait for the ramp to rest on the footpath.
evidence.scope: A TFI bus kneeling and deploying its ramp at a suitable stop.

questions.question: A passenger appears to have difficulty hearing your boarding instructions. What should you do when speaking to them?
options: Turn to face the road while repeating the instructions.
Give the instructions only to a person standing beside them.
Face the passenger and speak clearly.
questions.explanation: Facing and addressing the passenger directly makes communication easier, particularly if they use visual cues.

evidence.section: Section A, Hurrying loading/unloading passengers, p. 4
evidence.rationale: Facing and addressing the passenger directly makes communication easier, particularly if they use visual cues.
evidence.scope: Individual boarding assistance while the bus is stopped.

questions.question: You are running behind schedule. A stop is busy and boarding needs more time than planned. What should take priority?
options: Allow the time needed for safe boarding.
Start moving as soon as the doors can close to recover time.
Ask passengers to step on faster to meet the timetable.
questions.explanation: A timetable can create pressure to rush. Passenger safety and correct procedures take precedence.

evidence.section: Section A, Driving to schedule, p. 4
evidence.rationale: A timetable can create pressure to rush. Passenger safety and correct procedures take precedence.
evidence.scope: Ordinary service delay with safe boarding still in progress.

questions.question: A bag fits on an overhead rack but can slide out if the coach brakes. What should you do?
options: Leave it there if the passenger sits directly below it.
Ask the passenger to hold it in place only when the coach is turning.
Use a place or restraint that keeps the bag from moving.
questions.explanation: Carry-on luggage needs secure stowage so it cannot move and injure someone during braking or a collision.

evidence.rationale: Carry-on luggage needs secure stowage so it cannot move and injure someone during braking or a collision.
evidence.scope: A carry-on bag that is unsecured on an overhead rack.

questions.question: A passenger’s bag is too heavy or awkward for you to lift into the hold safely on your own. What should you do?
options: Lift it quickly to reduce the time you are holding it.
Twist towards the hold while lifting to avoid moving your feet.
Get suitable assistance or use an available handling aid.
questions.explanation: Plan the lift and get help or an aid if the load is beyond what you can safely manage.

evidence.section: Section A, Loading of luggage/goods, pp. 4–5
evidence.rationale: Plan the lift and get help or an aid if the load is beyond what you can safely manage.
evidence.scope: An awkward or heavy bag. Follow the operator’s handling procedure.

questions.question: A coach has working passenger seat belts. How can the operator inform seated passengers that they must use them while the coach is moving?
options: Use an announcement or the appropriate signs or other approved information method.
Mention it only if a passenger asks about a particular belt.
Use a notice in the driver’s paperwork which passengers cannot see.
questions.explanation: Passengers must be informed of the requirement. An announcement or appropriate signage can convey it.

evidence.section: Informing passengers of the need to wear a seat belt
evidence.rationale: Passengers must be informed of the requirement. An announcement or appropriate signage can convey it.
evidence.scope: Coach service with fitted belts. The question is about informing passengers.

questions.question: Your double-decker has reached the end of its final journey. The lower deck looks empty from your seat. What should you do before securing the bus?
options: Check only the lower deck because the upper deck cannot be seen from the cab.
Walk through both decks to check for remaining passengers and lost property.
Lock the bus and wait for a passenger to contact the depot if anything was left.
questions.explanation: A physical sweep of both decks helps find passengers who have stayed on board and items left behind.

evidence.rationale: A physical sweep of both decks helps find passengers who have stayed on board and items left behind.
evidence.scope: End-of-trip check before locking a double-decker.

questions.question: A coach will be unattended during a planned stop. An externally accessible luggage compartment can be locked. How should it be left?
options: Open a little for ventilation while passengers are away.
Unlocked so a passenger can collect bags without staff present.
Closed and locked against unauthorised access.
questions.explanation: The RSA advises securing accessible compartments when they can be locked. Follow the operator’s security checks.

evidence.rationale: The RSA advises securing accessible compartments when they can be locked. Follow the operator’s security checks.
evidence.scope: An unattended coach with lockable external compartments.

questions.question: Before leaving on a coach service with checked luggage, why reconcile the luggage with the passengers travelling?
options: To account for what was loaded and identify luggage that does not match the boarding records.
To estimate how many empty seats remain without counting passengers.
To replace the need for a secure luggage compartment.
questions.explanation: Reconciliation is a security and custody check. The operator should be able to account for loaded bags.

evidence.section: Section E, Accounting for luggage, p. 45
evidence.rationale: Reconciliation is a security and custody check. The operator should be able to account for loaded bags.
evidence.scope: An operation using checked luggage and the operator’s reconciliation procedure.

questions.question: On a fixed-stop bus service, a passenger asks you to open the doors between authorised stops for convenience. There is no emergency. What should you do?
options: Open the doors once the bus is stopped in traffic.
Let them off at any location provided they ask clearly.
Keep the doors closed and use an authorised stop.
questions.explanation: The RSA distinguishes normal boarding and alighting at authorised stops from emergency procedures and safe hail-and-ride operations.

evidence.section: Section C, Boarding and alighting, p. 27
evidence.rationale: The RSA distinguishes normal boarding and alighting at authorised stops from emergency procedures and safe hail-and-ride operations.
evidence.scope: Fixed-stop service, no emergency and no hail-and-ride provision.

questions.question: A passenger’s retractable belt pulls out but does not retract as designed. How should you record it?
options: As a defect for qualified assessment and repair.
As satisfactory because the webbing still comes out.
As a defect only if the belt is also visibly torn.
questions.explanation: A fitted belt must operate correctly as well as being free of damage. Failed retraction needs attention.

evidence.section: Section D, Roadworthiness and seat belt maintenance, p. 37
evidence.rationale: A fitted belt must operate correctly as well as being free of damage. Failed retraction needs attention.
evidence.scope: Passenger belt designed to retract automatically.

questions.question: An emergency exit door opens, but its warning buzzer fails the check. What is the right response?
options: Mark the whole check satisfactory because the door opens.
Report the failed warning as a defect.
Disable the alarm permanently so it cannot distract the driver.
questions.explanation: The walk-around check covers the emergency exit and its buzzer separately. A working door does not establish that its warning works.

evidence.section: Section A, Bus / PSV Driver Walk-Around Check Sheet, PSV checks
evidence.rationale: The walk-around check covers the emergency exit and its buzzer separately. A working door does not establish that its warning works.
evidence.scope: Bus with an emergency-exit buzzer fitted.

questions.question: Before departure you find a loose surface on a passenger entry step. What should you do?
options: Leave it because passengers can use the handrail.
Wait for someone to trip before deciding whether it matters.
Report it and have it made safe before using the step for boarding.
questions.explanation: Access steps and surfaces are checked for defects. A loose surface presents a trip hazard.

evidence.section: Section A, Bus / PSV Driver Walk-Around Check Sheet, vehicle access
evidence.rationale: Access steps and surfaces are checked for defects. A loose surface presents a trip hazard.
evidence.scope: Passenger access step with a loose surface.

questions.question: On level ground at normal ride height, an unfamiliar coach is visibly leaning to one side. What should you do?
options: Assume it is normal on all air-suspended coaches.
Load luggage on the opposite side until it appears level.
Have the abnormal lean investigated before taking the coach into service.
questions.explanation: The walk-around includes checking that the vehicle sits square. An unexplained lean needs assessment.

evidence.section: Section A, Bus / PSV Driver Walk-Around Check Sheet, external vehicle checks
evidence.rationale: The walk-around includes checking that the vehicle sits square. An unexplained lean needs assessment.
evidence.scope: Vehicle is on level ground and should be at normal ride height, not intentionally kneeling.

questions.question: You have finished loading luggage. What final exterior check concerns the luggage hold itself before you drive off?
options: Check only that the passengers’ seats are occupied.
Leave the door slightly open until the vehicle warms up.
Confirm the hold door is closed and latched securely.
questions.explanation: The pre-departure check includes securing the luggage door so it cannot open in transit.

evidence.section: Section A, Bus / PSV Driver Walk-Around Check Sheet, prior to leaving depot
evidence.rationale: The pre-departure check includes securing the luggage door so it cannot open in transit.
evidence.scope: Coach with an exterior luggage hold.

questions.question: Before a damp morning departure, the demister fails to direct air to the windscreen. How should you treat this?
options: Ignore it if the windscreen is clear while parked.
Drive and wipe the windscreen by hand whenever it fogs.
Report it as a defect affecting your ability to keep the windscreen clear.
questions.explanation: A working demister is part of the in-cab check. Visibility can deteriorate once the bus is in use.

evidence.section: Section A, Bus / PSV Driver Walk-Around Check Sheet, in-cab checks
evidence.rationale: A working demister is part of the in-cab check. Visibility can deteriorate once the bus is in use.
evidence.scope: Pre-use check with demister unable to clear the windscreen as intended.

questions.question: A fitted fire extinguisher has a pressure gauge. The needle is outside its serviceable range during the pre-use check. What should you do?
options: Report it for repair or replacement before the bus is driven.
Leave it in service if the safety pin is intact.
Shake the extinguisher and then use the bus as normal.
questions.explanation: An out-of-range gauge may indicate a discharged or faulty extinguisher. It needs attention before departure.

evidence.rationale: An out-of-range gauge may indicate a discharged or faulty extinguisher. It needs attention before departure.
evidence.scope: Extinguisher with a gauge showing pressure outside the safe range.

questions.question: A handrail next to the entrance moves when you check it. How should you respond?
options: Treat it as normal movement when passengers put weight on it.
Cover it with a sign and keep boarding people normally.
Report the loose handrail and have it made safe before passengers rely on it.
questions.explanation: Handrails are part of the passenger-area check. A loose one may fail when someone uses it for support.

evidence.section: Section A, Bus / PSV Driver Walk-Around Check Sheet, PSV checks
evidence.rationale: Handrails are part of the passenger-area check. A loose one may fail when someone uses it for support.
evidence.scope: A passenger grab rail that should be rigid is loose.

questions.question: Your coach has been evacuated because of smoke. Someone asks to get back on for a passport. What should you do?
options: Keep them away from the coach and tell responders what is needed.
Let them return if they know exactly where the passport is.
Send another passenger in to collect it quickly.
questions.explanation: The RSA advises keeping everyone out of an evacuated vehicle, including people seeking belongings.

evidence.rationale: The RSA advises keeping everyone out of an evacuated vehicle, including people seeking belongings.
evidence.scope: Coach evacuated because of smoke. Follow emergency responders’ directions.

questions.question: Everyone is clear of a coach and an engine-bay fire is suspected. Should you lift the engine cover to inspect it?
options: Yes, lift it fully so smoke can escape.
Yes, if another person films the condition for the operator.
No. Leave the engine cover closed and let the fire service deal with it.
questions.explanation: The RSA says to leave the cover of an engine fire for the fire brigade. Keep people clear.

evidence.rationale: The RSA says to leave the cover of an engine fire for the fire brigade. Keep people clear.
evidence.scope: Suspected engine-compartment fire after evacuation.

questions.question: Your bus is safely stopped and passengers are evacuating because of a fire. Where should you direct them if that location is accessible?
options: To a safe place upwind, well away from the bus and passing traffic.
Along the traffic lane so emergency responders can find them.
Immediately behind the bus so they can watch for smoke.
questions.explanation: An upwind location away from the bus and traffic reduces exposure to smoke and other hazards.

evidence.rationale: An upwind location away from the bus and traffic reduces exposure to smoke and other hazards.
evidence.scope: Evacuation location can be reached safely.

questions.question: When calling emergency services from safety about a bus fire, what passenger information is especially important?
options: Give only the number of seats on the vehicle.
Wait for an exact headcount before mentioning anyone still on board.
Tell them if anyone may still be on board.
questions.explanation: Tell responders your location and any known or suspected remaining passengers so they can plan the response.

evidence.rationale: Tell responders your location and any known or suspected remaining passengers so they can plan the response.
evidence.scope: Fire reported to emergency services from a safe place.

questions.question: A coach’s automatic engine-fire system activates. Why must the driver still stop safely and evacuate?
options: It covers the engine compartment and has limited capacity. The fire can recur.
It makes the vehicle safe to keep running until the next scheduled stop.
It means passengers elsewhere on the coach can remain without assessment.
questions.explanation: An automatic system can suppress an engine-bay fire, but it has limited coverage and the fire can reignite.

evidence.section: Section D, Engine Fire Suppression Systems, p. 33
evidence.rationale: An automatic system can suppress an engine-bay fire, but it has limited coverage and the fire can reignite.
evidence.scope: Activation indicating a possible fire on a vehicle fitted with engine-bay suppression.

questions.question: A coach has a designated break-glass exit with a fitted emergency hammer. What should you check before carrying passengers?
options: That the hammer is accessible at its intended location and the exit is identifiable.
That the hammer is locked in the luggage hold to prevent theft.
That a hammer is stored somewhere in the driver’s personal bag.
questions.explanation: The equipment must be readily available to use if the designated window is needed for evacuation.

evidence.section: Section D, Emergency window hammers and emergency exits, pp. 34–35
evidence.rationale: The equipment must be readily available to use if the designated window is needed for evacuation.
evidence.scope: A designated break-glass exit requiring the fitted tool.

questions.question: You begin a slow left turn in a coach with significant rear overhang. Which movement can endanger someone alongside the back of the coach?
options: The rear will always stay inside the front wheels’ path.
The rear can only move straight back.
The rear can swing out to the right.
questions.explanation: The rear overhang can swing opposite to the direction of the turn. Check clearance on that side before and during the manoeuvre.

evidence.rationale: The rear overhang can swing opposite to the direction of the turn. Check clearance on that side before and during the manoeuvre.
evidence.scope: Left turn in a coach with significant tail swing.

questions.question: When an articulated bus goes round a tight corner, how can the rear section’s path differ from the front’s?
options: It can cut in and take a shorter path around the bend.
It always follows the front wheels exactly.
It always moves further out than the front section throughout the turn.
questions.explanation: The rear section can take an inside path around a bend. Allow for the inside clearance as well as tail swing.

evidence.rationale: The rear section can take an inside path around a bend. Allow for the inside clearance as well as tail swing.
evidence.scope: An articulated bus negotiating a tight corner.

questions.question: A long, low coach is approaching a hump-back bridge. What should the driver assess in addition to width and overhead height?
options: Whether the destination display can be read from the bridge.
Whether the underside or overhang may ground as the coach crosses the crest.
Whether crossing faster will lift the vehicle over the crest.
questions.explanation: A sharp crest or ramp can cause grounding even where the route is wide and clear overhead.

evidence.section: Section C, Road Sharing, turning and grounding, p. 23
evidence.rationale: A sharp crest or ramp can cause grounding even where the route is wide and clear overhead.
evidence.scope: A low vehicle approaching a sharp crest. Assess the route before committing.

questions.question: Your bus reaches a yield sign where its contra-flow lane rejoins normal traffic. Who should give way?
options: You should give way to traffic on the road you are joining.
Other vehicles must wait because you were in a reserved lane.
You may merge first whenever the bus is indicating.
questions.explanation: The yield sign still controls the merge. A reserved lane does not confer priority beyond its end.

evidence.rationale: The yield sign still controls the merge. A reserved lane does not confer priority beyond its end.
evidence.scope: Bus merging at a signed yield point.

questions.question: You are in a continuous bus lane signed No Left Turn from Bus Lane. What does that sign mean for a bus in the lane?
options: Turn left whenever the neighbouring lane receives a green signal.
Use the left turn only when the bus is empty.
Do not turn left from that lane.
questions.explanation: The sign restricts the movement from the bus lane. Follow the authorised lane and turn arrangements.

evidence.rationale: The sign restricts the movement from the bus lane. Follow the authorised lane and turn arrangements.
evidence.scope: The No Left Turn from Bus Lane sign applies to the current lane.

questions.question: A sign and signals identify a toucan crossing. Which road users is that crossing designed for?
options: Pedestrians only; cyclists must always use a separate crossing.
Pedestrians and cyclists.
Buses and taxis using a reserved turning lane.
questions.explanation: A toucan crossing is designed to let pedestrians and cyclists cross under signal control.

evidence.rationale: A toucan crossing is designed to let pedestrians and cyclists cross under signal control.
evidence.scope: A signal-controlled toucan crossing.

questions.question: A left-turn arrow flashes amber and a cyclist in the adjacent cycle track is approaching the junction across your intended path. What should you do?
options: Give way and turn only when it is safe.
Turn first because an illuminated arrow always gives priority.
Treat the arrow as an instruction to wait for a steady red light.
questions.explanation: A flashing amber directional signal permits cautious movement subject to giving way to conflicting traffic, including cyclists.

evidence.section: Section 7, Traffic lights, flashing amber arrow, p. 109
evidence.rationale: A flashing amber directional signal permits cautious movement subject to giving way to conflicting traffic, including cyclists.
evidence.scope: A flashing amber directional arrow, not a steady green arrow or pelican signal.

questions.question: The main signal turns steady amber when you are already so close to the line that stopping would be dangerous. What does the RSA allow?
options: Always brake as hard as possible to stop behind the line.
Continue with care if stopping at the line would be dangerous.
Accelerate because amber gives unrestricted priority.
questions.explanation: The normal instruction is to stop. The exception applies where you are too close to stop safely when amber first appears.

evidence.rationale: The normal instruction is to stop. The exception applies where you are too close to stop safely when amber first appears.
evidence.scope: Steady amber first appears at an unsafe stopping distance.

questions.question: You find double yellow lines along a quiet street late at night. There is no sign indicating a special exemption. May you park there?
options: Yes, because no daytime restriction plate is present.
Yes, if you are ready to move when asked.
No. The double yellow lines prohibit parking at any time.
questions.explanation: Unlike a timed single yellow line, double yellow lines prohibit ordinary parking at any time.

evidence.rationale: Unlike a timed single yellow line, double yellow lines prohibit ordinary parking at any time.
evidence.scope: Ordinary parking without a relevant exemption.

questions.question: An Irish yellow diamond shows the silhouettes of two children. What should you expect?
options: A school ahead, where children may be near the road.
A playground for parking outside school hours.
A mandatory route for vehicles carrying children.
questions.explanation: The warning sign identifies a school ahead. Adjust your observation and speed for the conditions.

evidence.rationale: The warning sign identifies a school ahead. Adjust your observation and speed for the conditions.
evidence.scope: The standard yellow diamond warning sign showing two children.

questions.question: A motorway closure directs you to follow a solid triangle diversion. At the next junction, the signs show both a solid and an outline triangle. Which should you follow?
options: Either triangle, because the shape alone defines the route.
The solid triangle you were directed to follow.
The outline triangle, because it replaces the solid one after the first junction.
questions.explanation: The fill is part of the route symbol. Follow the assigned symbol through the diversion until you can rejoin the motorway.

evidence.section: Section 11, Emergency closure of sections on the motorway, p. 159
evidence.rationale: The fill is part of the route symbol. Follow the assigned symbol through the diversion until you can rejoin the motorway.
evidence.scope: A signed emergency diversion using distinct solid and outline symbols.

questions.question: At an unsigned junction of roads of equal importance, another driver is approaching from your right. Who should wait?
options: The driver on the right should wait because your vehicle is larger.
You should let traffic from the right pass before you proceed.
Whoever reaches the junction faster should go first.
questions.explanation: At a junction of equal roads, yield to traffic from your right and proceed cautiously once clear.

evidence.rationale: At a junction of equal roads, yield to traffic from your right and proceed cautiously once clear.
evidence.scope: No controlling sign, light, Garda, or major-road priority.

questions.question: You are turning right at an uncontrolled junction. An oncoming driver is turning left into the same road. Who should go first?
options: The oncoming driver turning left.
The driver turning right because the manoeuvre takes longer.
The vehicle with the longer wheelbase.
questions.explanation: When these two opposing turns conflict, the left-turning driver has priority. Wait before completing your right turn.

evidence.rationale: When these two opposing turns conflict, the left-turning driver has priority. Wait before completing your right turn.
evidence.scope: No signals or other controls alter the normal priority.

questions.question: You are driving out of a private depot entrance onto a public road. A vehicle is approaching on the public road. Who should yield?
options: You must yield to traffic on the public road.
The vehicle on the road must yield because you are leaving premises.
The first driver to indicate has priority.
questions.explanation: Entering from a private entrance does not give you priority over traffic already using the public road.

evidence.rationale: Entering from a private entrance does not give you priority over traffic already using the public road.
evidence.scope: Ordinary unsignalised private entrance.

questions.question: You are about to cross a busy road in a fully laden coach. Why might you need a larger gap than you would in a small car?
options: Drivers on the busy road must stop when they see the coach.
The whole coach needs time to clear the road and it may accelerate more slowly.
Only the front of the coach needs to clear the lane before other traffic reaches it.
questions.explanation: Allow for both the coach’s length and its acceleration. Wait for a gap that lets the complete vehicle clear safely.

evidence.section: Section G, Leaving space when crossing or merging, p. 48
evidence.rationale: Allow for both the coach’s length and its acceleration. Wait for a gap that lets the complete vehicle clear safely.
evidence.scope: Coach crossing a road where other traffic has priority.

questions.question: You are turning right at a yellow box on an ordinary road. The exit road is clear and waiting in the box would block nobody. May you enter while waiting for a gap in oncoming traffic?
options: No. The exception applies only to traffic going straight.
Yes, under the right-turn exception when it does not block traffic with priority.
Yes, even if the exit road fills and the vehicle will block crossing traffic.
questions.explanation: The limited right-turn exception covers waiting for oncoming traffic. Do not enter if you would block traffic with priority.

evidence.rationale: The limited right-turn exception covers waiting for oncoming traffic. Do not enter if you would block traffic with priority.
evidence.scope: Ordinary road junction, no rail or tram crossing, exit clear and nobody with priority blocked.

questions.question: A person is waiting at a zebra crossing and clearly intends to cross. You can stop safely. What does RSA driver guidance call for?
options: Continue because giving way is unnecessary until they reach the middle.
Slow down and give way so the person can cross safely.
Stop on the crossing itself to let them pass behind you.
questions.explanation: The driver guidance says to give way to people at a zebra crossing, including those waiting to cross.

evidence.rationale: The driver guidance says to give way to people at a zebra crossing, including those waiting to cross.
evidence.scope: RSA driver guidance for an obvious intent to cross. Stop safely before the crossing.

questions.question: Both motorway lanes are moving in slow queues. Your existing left lane is moving a little quicker than the right. May you keep progressing with your queue?
options: Yes. Progressing in your existing lane is allowed in these slow-moving queues.
No. Stop whenever any vehicle to your right falls behind.
Yes. Move into the left lane specifically to pass at normal motorway speed.
questions.explanation: The slow-queue exception allows the left queue to progress faster than the right. It is not permission to undertake in free-flowing traffic.

evidence.section: Section 11, Overtaking on the motorway, p. 153
evidence.rationale: The slow-queue exception allows the left queue to progress faster than the right. It is not permission to undertake in free-flowing traffic.
evidence.scope: Both lanes are moving in slow queues. Remain in the existing lane.

questions.question: A bus is designed to carry standing passengers but is empty today. On a road signed at 80 km/h, what vehicle limit applies?
options: 80 km/h because nobody is standing.
65 km/h.
100 km/h because it is running empty.
questions.explanation: The 65 km/h limit is tied to vehicle design, not how many passengers are aboard on that journey.

evidence.section: Section 8, Speed limits for vehicles, pp. 120–121
evidence.rationale: The 65 km/h limit is tied to vehicle design, not how many passengers are aboard on that journey.
evidence.scope: Bus designed for standing passengers. A lower road limit or conditions can require less.

questions.question: A coach designed for seated passengers only is on a dual carriageway signed at 100 km/h, and is towing nothing. What is its applicable vehicle limit there?
options: 65 km/h.
questions.explanation: A seated-only coach may travel up to 100 km/h on a dual carriageway where no lower limit applies.

evidence.section: Section 8, Speed limits for vehicles, pp. 120–121
evidence.rationale: A seated-only coach may travel up to 100 km/h on a dual carriageway where no lower limit applies.
evidence.scope: Seated-only coach, no trailer, dual carriageway, and no lower applicable limit.

questions.question: You drive a bus designed for standing passengers on a three-lane motorway. It has no standing passengers today and there is no obstruction. May you use the outermost lane for an ordinary overtake?
options: No. Its design still puts it in the restricted vehicle class.
Yes. Count only the people who are standing at that moment.
Yes, if you signal earlier than the other vehicles.
questions.explanation: The outside-lane restriction applies to the design class. Ordinary overtaking is not the obstruction exception.

evidence.rationale: The outside-lane restriction applies to the design class. Ordinary overtaking is not the obstruction exception.
evidence.scope: Vehicle designed for standing passengers. No obstruction and no contrary direction.

questions.question: Visibility drops sharply as you enter dense fog on a dual carriageway. What lighting and speed response does the RSA advise?
options: Use main beam and maintain the speed of surrounding traffic.
Switch to sidelights alone and follow the lights ahead closely.
Use dipped headlights, reduce speed and use fog lamps as appropriate.
questions.explanation: Dense fog calls for lower speed and suitable lighting. Dipped headlights help without the glare associated with main beam.

evidence.rationale: Dense fog calls for lower speed and suitable lighting. Dipped headlights help without the glare associated with main beam.
evidence.scope: Dense fog, fog lamps used in accordance with their permitted conditions.

questions.question: You pass parked vehicles near shops and see movement between two of them at kerb level. What should you anticipate?
options: Any pedestrian must wait until you have passed because the road is busy.
The parked vehicles will prevent anyone from entering the road.
A pedestrian could emerge into the road with little warning.
questions.explanation: Parked vehicles can hide people until they step out. Reduce speed and allow space to respond.

evidence.rationale: Parked vehicles can hide people until they step out. Reduce speed and allow space to respond.
evidence.scope: Possible pedestrian movement concealed by parked vehicles.

questions.question: What does swan-necking describe when a long coach is taking a right turn?
options: Allowing extra space for the rear wheels to track inside the front wheels.
Passing the appropriate turning point and needing a sharper correction to finish the turn.
Using a marked left-turn lane to approach a junction.
questions.explanation: Plan the turning path so you do not overshoot the appropriate point and have to make a sharper correction.

evidence.rationale: Plan the turning path so you do not overshoot the appropriate point and have to make a sharper correction.
evidence.scope: A right turn by a long vehicle where the driver can plan the path.

questions.question: You are about to pull away from a busy bus stop. What should you check besides the traffic in the lane you intend to join?
options: Only the passengers seated on the upper deck.
The area immediately alongside the bus for people approaching or still close to it.
Only the timetable display and the signal light.
questions.explanation: Check mirrors and relevant blind spots around the bus before moving away, including the area near passengers.

evidence.section: Section G, Moving off and use of mirrors, p. 45
evidence.rationale: Check mirrors and relevant blind spots around the bus before moving away, including the area near passengers.
evidence.scope: Routine departure from a busy stop after boarding has finished.

questions.question: An operator’s procedure warns that the exhaust is still very hot. Which place should you avoid when parking a bus?
options: A properly designated bay with a clean hard surface.
An open area that meets the operator’s parking procedure.
Over dry vegetation or other easily ignited material.
questions.explanation: Hot exhaust components can ignite combustible material beneath the vehicle.

evidence.section: Section G, Fire risk from exhaust temperatures
evidence.rationale: Hot exhaust components can ignite combustible material beneath the vehicle.
evidence.scope: Bus with a hot exhaust system. Follow the vehicle and operator guidance.

questions.question: A road tunnel is lit throughout. Which headlights should you use when driving through it?
options: Main beam because the walls are close.
Dipped headlights.
Daytime running lights alone because the tunnel is lit.
questions.explanation: RSA tunnel guidance calls for dipped headlights while driving in the tunnel.

evidence.rationale: RSA tunnel guidance calls for dipped headlights while driving in the tunnel.
evidence.scope: Normal driving in a road tunnel.

questions.question: After a motorway breakdown, you can safely use a roadside emergency telephone. What location advantage does it provide?
options: The telephone automatically sends your vehicle’s registration.
The call identifies the telephone’s location to the motorway control centre.
The telephone means no one needs to explain the nature of the incident.
questions.explanation: Using the roadside emergency phone lets the control centre identify the call location automatically. Explain what has happened.

evidence.section: Section 11, What to do if your vehicle breaks down, p. 157
evidence.rationale: Using the roadside emergency phone lets the control centre identify the call location automatically. Explain what has happened.
evidence.scope: A roadside emergency phone can be reached and used safely.

questions.question: You are involved in a road collision and another person involved requests the required details. No Garda is at the scene. Which information belongs in the exchange?
options: Only the scheduled destination and passenger count.
The vehicle registration and evidence of insurance, along with the required identity and address information.
Only the name of the employer and the route number.
questions.explanation: The RSA lists the vehicle registration and insurance information among the details drivers must give after a collision.

evidence.section: Section 14, What drivers must do at an incident or in an emergency, p. 179
evidence.rationale: The RSA lists the vehicle registration and insurance information among the details drivers must give after a collision.
evidence.scope: A person involved requests details when no Garda is present.

questions.question: Before a night service, passenger aisle lighting that should work is out. How should the driver respond?
options: Rely on passengers to use their phone lights.
Treat the check as satisfactory if the headlamps work.
Report the lighting defect and have safe use assessed before departure.
questions.explanation: The check covers lighting in the passenger area. Working exterior lamps do not establish that the interior is safe.

evidence.section: Section A, Bus / PSV Driver Walk-Around Check Sheet, PSV checks
evidence.rationale: The check covers lighting in the passenger area. Working exterior lamps do not establish that the interior is safe.
evidence.scope: Bus with failed passenger-area lighting before a night service.

questions.question: A coach requires a first-aid kit. The box is present, but its contents are past their service dates. What should the walk-around establish?
options: That the kit is properly stocked, in date and ready to use.
That the box has a label, regardless of the contents.
That the kit is locked away from passengers during a routine inspection.
questions.explanation: Presence alone is insufficient. Check that required supplies are in date and available for use.

evidence.section: Section A, Completion of daily checks, p. 5
evidence.rationale: Presence alone is insufficient. Check that required supplies are in date and available for use.
evidence.scope: Coach with a required first-aid kit and dated contents.

questions.question: A coach has been held back by continuous use of its service brakes on a long descent. Why can the brakes become less effective?
options: The road speed limit changes the pressure in the tyres.
Heat builds up in the brakes and can cause brake fade.
The brakes become more effective as their temperature rises without limit.
questions.explanation: Prolonged service braking can overheat the brakes and reduce the braking effort available.

evidence.rationale: Prolonged service braking can overheat the brakes and reduce the braking effort available.
evidence.scope: Long descent and repeated or continuous use of service brakes.

questions.question: You have time to slow for a normal stop with standing passengers aboard. Why is progressive braking important?
options: It keeps passengers upright by causing them to move quickly forward.
It reduces the sudden forward movement that can make standing passengers lose balance.
It makes it safe to approach the stop at a higher speed.
questions.explanation: People continue moving relative to the bus as it slows. Progressive braking limits the abrupt change they have to resist.

evidence.section: Section H, Effects of acceleration, braking and cornering on passengers, p. 56
evidence.rationale: People continue moving relative to the bus as it slows. Progressive braking limits the abrupt change they have to resist.
evidence.scope: Planned stop with time for smooth braking. Immediate hazards may require firmer braking.

questions.question: What direction do passengers tend to move relative to the bus if it takes a curve too quickly?
options: Towards the outside of the curve.
Towards the inside of the curve.
Directly backwards, regardless of the curve.
