questions.explanation: A sharp turn can throw passengers and loose objects towards the outside of the curve.

evidence.rationale: A sharp turn can throw passengers and loose objects towards the outside of the curve.
evidence.scope: A bus cornering too quickly. Allow for road conditions and passengers.

questions.question: Why is it generally better to reduce speed before a bend than rely on heavy braking while already turning?
options: Braking and turning together demand grip from the same tyres.
Tyre grip automatically increases once the bus begins turning.
The steering and brakes use separate road surfaces, so their demands do not interact.
questions.explanation: The tyres have a limited amount of grip. Heavy braking while turning can exceed what is available.

evidence.section: Section B, Loss of Control, p. 19
evidence.rationale: The tyres have a limited amount of grip. Heavy braking while turning can exceed what is available.
evidence.scope: Planned approach to a bend where speed can be reduced early.

questions.question: During emergency braking in a coach with working ABS, you feel the brake pedal pulsate. Under the cited guidance, what should you do while full emergency braking is still needed?
options: Pump the pedal in time with the pulses.
Maintain firm brake pressure and let the system manage wheel lock.
Release the pedal completely until the pulses stop.
questions.explanation: The pulses can be caused by the system varying pressure. For a vehicle whose instructions match the RSA guidance, keep emergency braking pressure applied.

evidence.section: Section H, Correct use of ABS, p. 58
evidence.rationale: The pulses can be caused by the system varying pressure. For a vehicle whose instructions match the RSA guidance, keep emergency braking pressure applied.
evidence.scope: Working ABS during emergency braking. Follow the manufacturer’s instructions for the vehicle.

questions.question: What is one advantage of a working electronically controlled braking system on a coach?
options: It stops the vehicle without any need for tyre grip.
It makes the service brake redundant whenever passengers are standing.
It can reduce the time between pressing the pedal and applying braking effort at the wheels.
questions.explanation: The electronic signal can reduce activation time and help distribute braking effort across the wheels.

evidence.section: Section H, Electronically controlled Braking System, p. 58
evidence.rationale: The electronic signal can reduce activation time and help distribute braking effort across the wheels.
evidence.scope: A coach fitted with working EBS. Actual stopping distance still depends on conditions.

questions.question: In the manual gearbox described by the RSA, when should you select reverse?
options: While it is still rolling forwards slowly.
While it is coasting down a gradient.
When the bus is stationary.
questions.explanation: The RSA describes selecting reverse only with the vehicle stationary. Follow the manual for the actual gearbox.

evidence.rationale: The RSA describes selecting reverse only with the vehicle stationary. Follow the manual for the actual gearbox.
evidence.scope: Manual bus gearbox covered by the cited guidance.

questions.question: You are waiting on a hill in a bus with an automated manual transmission. Why should you use its approved hill-hold or parking-brake procedure rather than holding it with the accelerator?
options: Keeping the accelerator partly down is the intended way to secure the bus indefinitely.
Selecting neutral on its own holds the bus on a gradient.
The proper holding system prevents movement without relying on the transmission to hold the bus.
questions.explanation: Use the manufacturer’s specified parking-brake or hill-holding procedure when stationary on a gradient.

evidence.section: Section H, Automated Manual Transmission, p. 54
evidence.rationale: Use the manufacturer’s specified parking-brake or hill-holding procedure when stationary on a gradient.
evidence.scope: Automated manual transmission. Use the exact vehicle and operator procedure.

questions.question: A coach driver checks the vehicle against its maximum authorised mass before a tour. Which items must be included in the laden vehicle weight?
options: The vehicle, driver, passengers, fuel and luggage.
The vehicle and luggage only.
The vehicle and passengers, excluding fuel and the driver.
questions.explanation: Maximum authorised mass limits the complete loaded vehicle. People and fuel contribute to the actual laden weight.

evidence.section: Section D, Calculation of payload and load distribution, p. 27
evidence.rationale: Maximum authorised mass limits the complete loaded vehicle. People and fuel contribute to the actual laden weight.
evidence.scope: The whole laden coach. Axle limits are separate checks.

questions.question: A tour group arrives with unusually heavy equipment and you are uncertain whether the coach remains within its weights. What is the useful check before driving?
options: Establish the loaded weight and axle distribution, using a suitable weighbridge if available.
Count the passengers and assume the load is legal if seats remain.
Use the weight recorded before the luggage was added.
questions.explanation: The nature of the trip affects the load. Verify the actual loaded weights when estimates leave doubt.

evidence.section: Section D, What can a driver do to ensure that the vehicle is not overloaded, p. 28
evidence.rationale: The nature of the trip affects the load. Verify the actual loaded weights when estimates leave doubt.
evidence.scope: Passenger coach carrying unusual heavy luggage. Follow the operator’s load plan.

questions.question: A long-front-overhang coach is manoeuvring between walls. Why is the wheel turning circle alone insufficient for judging clearance?
options: The front bodywork is always inside the wheel path.
The front bodywork can extend beyond the path of the front wheels.
The turning circle accounts only for the back of the coach.
questions.explanation: The front body extends ahead of the axle and can sweep a larger space than the wheel path suggests.

evidence.rationale: The front body extends ahead of the axle and can sweep a larger space than the wheel path suggests.
evidence.scope: Low-speed manoeuvre with close walls and a large front overhang.

questions.question: A minibus is built for 16 passengers in addition to the driver, but is 8.5 metres long. Does it meet the D1 vehicle length limit?
options: Yes. Passenger capacity is the only D1 limit.
No. The D1 vehicle length limit is 8 metres.
Yes. The length limit applies only when a trailer is attached.
questions.explanation: The D1 category limits both passenger capacity and vehicle length. Meeting the seating condition does not remove the length condition.

evidence.section: Driving licence categories in Ireland, D1
evidence.rationale: The D1 category limits both passenger capacity and vehicle length. Meeting the seating condition does not remove the length condition.
evidence.scope: D1 vehicle entitlement, no trailer and no exceptional licence conditions.

questions.question: What can a large concentration of passenger weight high in a double-decker do to its stability?
options: Raise the centre of gravity and make the vehicle more sensitive to sideways forces.
Lower the centre of gravity because the upper deck is heavier.
Remove the effect of cornering speed as long as the lower deck is empty.
questions.explanation: Putting more weight high in the bus raises its centre of gravity. Allow for the vehicle’s stability and load when driving.

evidence.section: Section B, Stability test and lateral stability, p. 20
evidence.rationale: Putting more weight high in the bus raises its centre of gravity. Allow for the vehicle’s stability and load when driving.
evidence.scope: General stability principle. Carry passengers only within the approved vehicle capacity.

questions.question: An in-scope driver is on one seven-day occasional passenger service and drives no more than seven hours that day. If all other conditions for the occasional-service daily-rest option are met, how often can the 25-hour window be used on that service?
options: Twice, because the service lasts more than six days.
Once.
Every day on which driving stays below seven hours.
questions.explanation: The option can be used once on a qualifying service of at least six consecutive 24-hour periods. Twice requires at least eight such periods.

evidence.rationale: The option can be used once on a qualifying service of at least six consecutive 24-hour periods. Twice requires at least eight such periods.
evidence.scope: A single service of seven consecutive 24-hour periods with the other safety and working-time conditions met.

questions.question: A driver wants to rely on the occasional-service split-break option and uses paper documentation under the regulation. What should they have on board for that service?
options: A completed journey form containing the required information for the service.
A blank journey form to complete only if stopped.
A copy of the driver’s licence as a substitute for the journey form.
questions.explanation: For the paper-documentation route the form for the service is completed before the journey. Other record requirements can also apply.

evidence.rationale: For the paper-documentation route the form for the service is completed before the journey. Other record requirements can also apply.
evidence.scope: Occasional passenger service using the specified derogation and the paper documentation route.

questions.question: An in-scope driver is lawfully continuing temporarily after a tachograph card is stolen. What record should they make at the start and end of the journey?
options: Use a colleague’s card to avoid making printouts.
Use tachograph printouts and add the required identification and unrecorded activities.
Wait for the replacement card and record nothing in the meantime.
questions.explanation: Without the card, the regulation requires printouts and the specified manual information and signatures.

evidence.rationale: Without the card, the regulation requires printouts and the specified manual information and signatures.
evidence.scope: Temporary continuation after theft under the applicable limits. The regulation’s declaration and replacement duties still apply.

questions.question: An occasional coach operator wants to postpone a weekly rest under the conditional 12-day provision. What kind of weekly rest must precede the period used for that option?
options: Any reduced daily rest of nine hours.
A regular weekly rest.
A single 45-minute driving break.
questions.explanation: The derogation is measured from a previous regular weekly rest and is subject to other eligibility and follow-up conditions.

evidence.rationale: The derogation is measured from a previous regular weekly rest and is subject to other eligibility and follow-up conditions.
evidence.scope: Qualifying single occasional passenger service. The question asks only about the preceding rest.

questions.question: A coach is booked for a dedicated school outing carrying a group of children. What should the operator verify before assigning it?
options: The coach has the appropriate fitted seat belts for the number of children carried.
Belts are needed only if the trip crosses a county boundary.
The number of belts is irrelevant if the trip starts at a school.
questions.explanation: A vehicle used for organised transport of children needs appropriate belts for the children carried.

evidence.section: What is the law on carrying children in buses?
evidence.rationale: A vehicle used for organised transport of children needs appropriate belts for the children carried.
evidence.scope: Dedicated organised group trip covered by the Irish rules.

questions.question: A city bus designed for standing passengers is operating its ordinary city route and is not used for organised transport of children. Does the RSA describe an exemption from fitting passenger seat belts for this case?
options: Yes, the ordinary city-bus category is treated differently from a bus used for organised transport of children.
No, every city bus must retrofit belts before it can carry passengers.
Yes, and the exemption also applies to any coach hired for a dedicated school outing.
questions.explanation: The RSA describes the city-bus fitting exemption and the distinct requirement for organised transport of children.

evidence.section: Do all buses have to be fitted with seat belts?
evidence.rationale: The RSA describes the city-bus fitting exemption and the distinct requirement for organised transport of children.
evidence.scope: Ordinary city service, not organised transport of children. Concerns fitting, not use of a belt where fitted.

questions.question: A passenger asks how a fitted lap belt should lie across them. Which guidance is appropriate?
options: High across the abdomen and left slack.
Low across the hips and properly tightened.
Under one leg so they can release it more easily.
questions.explanation: A lap belt should restrain at the hips. A high or loose belt can work less effectively and cause injury.

evidence.section: How to wear lap belts correctly
evidence.rationale: A lap belt should restrain at the hips. A high or loose belt can work less effectively and cause injury.
evidence.scope: Coach seat fitted with a lap belt. Follow the instructions for the actual restraint.

questions.question: At a safe stop, a passenger is upset about a service problem and asks for help. What is the most appropriate initial response?
options: Argue immediately about who caused the problem.
Listen calmly and identify the problem before explaining what can be done.
Dismiss the concern until the passenger leaves the bus.
questions.explanation: The RSA customer guidance advises listening and understanding the concern before proposing a fair response.

evidence.section: Section C, How to respond to a customer with a complaint, p. 27
evidence.rationale: The RSA customer guidance advises listening and understanding the concern before proposing a fair response.
evidence.scope: A complaint, without an immediate threat requiring emergency procedures.

questions.question: You have begun driving a right-hand-drive coach in a country where traffic keeps right. What should you account for before attempting an overtake?
options: The seating position makes the view past any vehicle ahead better than in Ireland.
The seating position can limit your view past the vehicle ahead, so stay back and make careful observations.
The usual view from the cab is unchanged if you sit closer to the vehicle ahead.
questions.explanation: The RSA warns that the driver’s position can make it harder to see past vehicles where traffic keeps right. Allow more room to see and decide.

evidence.section: Section G, Driving in mainland Europe, p. 50
evidence.rationale: The RSA warns that the driver’s position can make it harder to see past vehicles where traffic keeps right. Allow more room to see and decide.
evidence.scope: A right-hand-drive coach in a country that drives on the right. Follow local rules.

questions.question: On a clear level road in a manual coach, which gear-choice principle supports economical driving?
options: Use a suitably high gear without making the engine labour.
Use the lowest gear that can maintain the speed.
Select the highest gear even if the engine struggles.
questions.explanation: The RSA advises using a high gear that suits the load and speed without labouring the engine.

evidence.rationale: The RSA advises using a high gear that suits the load and speed without labouring the engine.
evidence.scope: Manual coach and stable road conditions. Follow the vehicle’s operating guidance.

questions.question: You must walk from a parked coach to the depot office. There is a marked pedestrian walkway and buses are manoeuvring nearby. Which route should you take?
options: Use the designated pedestrian walkway.
Walk through the manoeuvring area so you can take the shortest route.
Walk closely behind a moving coach so its driver can see you.
questions.explanation: A designated walkway keeps pedestrians away from bus manoeuvres and blind areas.

evidence.rationale: A designated walkway keeps pedestrians away from bus manoeuvres and blind areas.
evidence.scope: Depot with a designated walkway.

questions.question: An ordinary motorist plans to park in an area marked BUS while waiting for a friend. What does that marking mean for their plan?
options: They should find a lawful parking place clear of the marked bus stop.
They may wait in the marked area as long as their engine is running.
They may park if they leave space at the front edge of the markings.
questions.explanation: The marked area is a bus stop and is not available for ordinary parking.

evidence.rationale: The marked area is a bus stop and is not available for ordinary parking.
evidence.scope: Marked bus stop and ordinary private vehicle parking.

questions.question: A street has no yellow lines, but the kerb has been lowered to provide wheelchair access. May you park across the lowered section?
options: Yes, if no wheelchair user is currently approaching.
Yes, if at least one wheel is on the kerb rather than the road.
No. Keep the lowered crossing point available.
questions.explanation: The parking rules keep lowered kerbs used for wheelchair access clear even without a yellow line.

evidence.rationale: The parking rules keep lowered kerbs used for wheelchair access clear even without a yellow line.
evidence.scope: Kerb lowered for wheelchair users.

questions.question: A school-zone sign displays an illuminated periodic speed limit of 30 km/h. What should you do while that limit applies?
options: Treat 30 km/h as advisory unless you see a child.
Use the usual road limit whenever a school warden is absent.
Treat 30 km/h as the maximum for the signed period, subject to conditions.
questions.explanation: A periodic regulatory limit is binding while in force. Conditions can require a slower speed.

evidence.rationale: A periodic regulatory limit is binding while in force. Conditions can require a slower speed.
evidence.scope: Active regulatory periodic limit.

questions.question: A parking bay displays the wheelchair symbol. You are driving a vehicle that is not carrying or collecting the permit holder and have no valid permit to use the bay. May you park there?
options: Yes, if you remain in the driver’s seat.
No. Leave the reserved bay for eligible use.
Yes, if you use the bay for less than five minutes.
questions.explanation: The marked bay is reserved for eligible use under the disability parking permit scheme.

evidence.rationale: The marked bay is reserved for eligible use under the disability parking permit scheme.
evidence.scope: Ordinary parking without a permit or an eligible passenger.

questions.question: After an incident involving your vehicle, what must you do at the scene even if you believe the damage is minor?
options: Stop and remain at the scene for a reasonable time.
Leave immediately and see whether anyone contacts you.
Drive on unless another driver signals for you to stop.
questions.explanation: Drivers involved in an incident must stop. Remaining allows them to check for assistance needs and fulfil their obligations.

evidence.section: Section 14, What drivers must do at an incident or in an emergency, p. 179
evidence.rationale: Drivers involved in an incident must stop. Remaining allows them to check for assistance needs and fulfil their obligations.
evidence.scope: Driver involved in an incident. Provide assistance and details as applicable.
